questions.question: Under IFRS 15, the transaction price may be adjusted for the effects of the time value of money when

options.a: the contract contains more than one performance obligation
options.b: the customer pays in a foreign currency
options.c: the contract includes a significant financing component
options.d: the stand-alone selling price is not observable

questions.explanation: When a contract includes a significant financing component, the transaction price may be adjusted for the time value of money. Option B is a currency issue, not a financing one. Option A leads to allocation in Step 4, and option D means the stand-alone selling price must be estimated.

questions.question: Where a contract has several performance obligations, IFRS 15 requires the transaction price to be allocated to them by reference to their

options.a: order of delivery to the customer

questions.explanation: The transaction price is allocated in proportion to the stand-alone selling price of each distinct good or service. Option B is wrong because allocation is based on selling prices, not costs. Options A and D ignore the value of each item, so they would not show the consideration the entity expects for each one.

questions.question: If the stand-alone selling price of a promised good is not observable, the entity should

options.b: allocate the whole transaction price to that good
options.d: treat the good as not distinct

questions.explanation: When a stand-alone selling price cannot be observed, the entity estimates it and then allocates on the relative basis as usual. Option A would understate revenue for a real performance obligation, and option B ignores the other obligations. Option D is wrong because being distinct depends on the distinct criteria, not on whether a price is observable.

questions.question: A package of goods is sold for less than the total of their stand-alone selling prices, and the discount does not relate to any specific performance obligation. How is the discount treated?

options.a: It is allocated to all the performance obligations on a stand-alone selling price basis
options.b: It is allocated entirely to the item delivered last
options.c: It is recognised as an expense when the package is sold
options.d: It is allocated entirely to the most expensive item

questions.explanation: A discount that does not relate to a specific performance obligation is shared across all of them in proportion to their stand-alone selling prices. Option D and option B load the whole discount onto one item for no reason. Option C is wrong because the discount reduces the transaction price; it is not an expense.

questions.question: Having the ability to direct the use of, and obtain the remaining benefits from, an asset is the IFRS 15 meaning of
questions.explanation: Control means the ability to direct the use of an asset and obtain the remaining benefits from it, and revenue is recognised when control passes. Options A and C are only indicators that control may have passed; a customer can have one without full control. Option B is a Step 1 contract criterion.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an indicator that control of an asset has passed to the customer at a point in time?

options.a: The customer has significant risks and rewards of ownership
options.b: The customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits as the entity performs
options.c: The customer has accepted the asset
options.d: The entity has a present right to payment for the asset

questions.explanation: Simultaneous receipt and consumption of benefits is a criterion for recognising revenue over time, not an indicator of a point-in-time transfer. Options A, C and D are all point-in-time indicators, along with legal title and transfer of physical possession.

questions.question: Which of the following indicates that control of goods has passed to the customer at a point in time?

options.a: The customer has legal title to the goods
options.b: The entity's performance creates an asset with no alternative use
options.d: The goods can benefit the customer together with readily available resources

questions.explanation: Legal title is one of the indicators that control has passed at a point in time, with physical possession, a present right to payment, risks and rewards of ownership and customer acceptance. Option C is a Step 1 contract criterion and option D is a Step 2 distinct test. Option B is part of an over-time criterion.

questions.question: Under IFRS 15, which pattern of revenue recognition is typical for each type of promise?

options.a: Both goods and services are always recognised at a point in time
options.b: Both goods and services are always recognised over time
options.c: Goods are typically recognised at a point in time; services typically over time
options.d: Goods are typically recognised over time; services at a point in time

questions.explanation: Transfers of goods are typically recognised at a point in time, while promises to transfer services are typically recognised over time, depending on the nature of the obligation. Option D reverses the two. Options A and B are wrong because the timing depends on the nature of each obligation, not a single rule for everything.

questions.question: GuardSafe Ltd provides security guards for an estate in Lekki for 12 months. The residents benefit from the protection each day as it is provided. On what basis should GuardSafe recognise revenue?

options.a: Over time, because the customer has legal title to the service
options.b: At a point in time, when the 12-month contract ends
options.c: Over time, because the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefit as the entity performs
options.d: At a point in time, when the contract is signed

questions.explanation: Security services are consumed as they are provided, which meets the over-time criterion of simultaneous receipt and consumption of benefits. Option B delays revenue even though the service is transferred daily, and option D recognises revenue before any performance. Option A wrongly uses a point-in-time indicator, legal title, to justify over-time recognition.

questions.question: BuildRight Ltd is constructing an office block on land owned and controlled by its customer in Abuja. As each floor is built, it belongs to the customer. Which criterion supports recognising revenue over time?

options.a: The contract has been approved by both parties
options.b: The customer will have physical possession when the building is completed
options.c: The customer will accept the building at the end of the contract
options.d: The entity's performance creates or enhances an asset that the customer controls as it is created

questions.explanation: When the entity's work creates or enhances an asset that the customer already controls, revenue is recognised over time as the work is done. Options B and C are point-in-time indicators that would only apply at completion. Option A is a Step 1 contract criterion and says nothing about timing.

questions.question: Ekiti Fabrication Ltd is making a machine built to one customer's unique specification; it could not be sold to anyone else. The contract gives Ekiti Fabrication an enforceable right to payment for work completed to date. How should revenue be recognised?

options.a: Over time, because the customer simultaneously consumes the machine
options.b: At a point in time, when the contract is signed
options.c: Over time, because the asset has no alternative use and there is an enforceable right to payment for work done
options.d: At a point in time, only when the machine is delivered

questions.explanation: An entity recognises revenue over time when its performance creates an asset with no alternative use to it and it has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date, and both conditions are met here. Option D ignores that the over-time criterion is met. Option B recognises revenue before any work, and option A is wrong because a machine is not consumed as it is built.

questions.question: A customer buys a generator from a shop in Alaba Market, pays in full, receives the receipt and carries the generator home. When should the shop recognise the revenue?

options.a: At the point of sale, when the customer obtains control of the generator
options.b: Only when the customer starts using the generator
options.c: Over the warranty period, on a straight-line basis
options.d: Over the generator's expected useful life

questions.explanation: The customer has paid, has legal title and has physical possession, so control passes at that point in time and revenue is recognised then. Options C and D wrongly spread revenue for goods that were transferred at once. Option B is wrong because recognition depends on transfer of control, not on when the customer chooses to use the asset.

questions.question: For a performance obligation satisfied over time, how does an entity determine how much revenue to recognise in each period?

options.a: It recognises revenue only when cash is received
options.b: It recognises all the revenue when the obligation is fully satisfied
options.c: It selects an appropriate measure of progress towards complete satisfaction of the obligation
options.d: It recognises all the revenue when the contract is signed

questions.explanation: For an over-time obligation, revenue is recognised to the extent the obligation has been fulfilled, using an appropriate measure of progress. Option D recognises revenue before any performance and option A ties revenue to cash rather than performance. Option B treats the obligation as if it were satisfied at a point in time.

questions.question: Kode Ltd sells a software licence and 12 months of support as a bundle for N1,800,000. Sold separately, the licence sells for N1,500,000 and the support for N500,000. How much of the transaction price is allocated to the licence?
questions.explanation: Total stand-alone selling prices are N2,000,000, so the licence gets 1,500,000/2,000,000 x N1,800,000 = N1,350,000. Option A uses the stand-alone price and ignores the bundle discount, while option D deducts support at full price so that the whole discount falls on the licence. Option C splits the price equally instead of on relative stand-alone selling prices.

questions.question: A Computer Village retailer sells a laptop and a printer together for N900,000. It normally sells the laptop for N750,000 and the printer for N450,000. How much of the transaction price is allocated to the printer?
questions.explanation: Total stand-alone selling prices are N1,200,000, so the printer gets 450,000/1,200,000 x N900,000 = N337,500. Option D is the printer's full stand-alone price, ignoring the N300,000 package discount. Option C gives the printer only what is left after the laptop's full price, and option B is the laptop's allocation.

questions.question: A Lekki store sells a phone (stand-alone price N400,000) and earbuds (stand-alone price N100,000) together for N450,000. The discount does not relate to either item specifically. How much of the discount is allocated to the earbuds?
questions.explanation: The N50,000 discount is shared in proportion to stand-alone prices, so the earbuds take 100,000/500,000 x N50,000 = N10,000, and are allocated N90,000 of the price. Option A puts the whole discount on the earbuds and option C puts none on them. Option B splits the discount equally instead of by relative stand-alone selling prices.

questions.question: In a package where a computer (stand-alone price N500,000) and a printer (stand-alone price N300,000) are sold together for N700,000, what is the total discount to be allocated across the two performance obligations?
questions.explanation: The discount is the total of the stand-alone selling prices less the package price: N800,000 - N700,000 = N100,000, which is then shared on a stand-alone selling price basis. Options D and C are the shares of that discount falling on the computer (N62,500) and the printer (N37,500), not the total. Option B wrongly deducts the printer's price from the computer's.

questions.question: A bundle contains item X (stand-alone price N600,000) and item Y (stand-alone price N400,000) and is sold for N900,000. What percentage of the transaction price is allocated to item X?
questions.explanation: The allocation ratio is item X's stand-alone price over the total stand-alone prices: 600,000/1,000,000 = 60%, so X receives N540,000. Option A wrongly divides by the transaction price (600,000/900,000). Option B is item Y's ratio, and option D ignores the different stand-alone prices.

questions.question: SolarTech Ltd sells a solar system for N2,400,000, which includes the equipment, installation and one year of maintenance. Stand-alone selling prices are: equipment N2,000,000, installation N500,000 and maintenance N500,000. How much is allocated to installation?
questions.explanation: Total stand-alone selling prices are N3,000,000, so installation gets 500,000/3,000,000 x N2,400,000 = N400,000. Option A ignores the N600,000 bundle discount. Option C splits the price equally between three items, and option B is the equipment's allocation.

questions.question: A software contract is priced at N3,150,000 and covers a licence, installation, updates and technical support. Stand-alone selling prices are: licence N2,000,000, installation N400,000, updates N600,000 and support N1,200,000. How much is allocated to technical support?
questions.explanation: Total stand-alone selling prices are N4,200,000, so support gets 1,200,000/4,200,000 x N3,150,000 = N900,000. Option D is support's full stand-alone price, ignoring the N1,050,000 discount. Option C splits the price equally across the four items, and option B is the licence's allocation.

questions.question: In a software contract, N900,000 of the transaction price is allocated to technical support to be provided evenly over five years. How much revenue from technical support is recognised in the first year?
questions.explanation: Technical support is a service transferred evenly over five years, so revenue is recognised over time: N900,000/5 = N180,000 per year. Option B recognises all of it at once, as if it were a point-in-time sale, and option C defers it all until the end. Option D spreads the amount over 12 months and takes only one month, instead of a full year out of five.

questions.question: On 1 October 2025, a telecom company sells a phone plus 12 months of data for N400,000. Stand-alone prices are phone N300,000 and data plan N200,000. The phone is handed over on 1 October; data is provided evenly. How much revenue is recognised for the year ended 31 December 2025?
questions.explanation: The phone gets 300,000/500,000 x N400,000 = N240,000, recognised at once when control passes, and the data plan gets N160,000, recognised over time: 3/12 x N160,000 = N40,000. Total revenue is N280,000. Option C uses stand-alone prices without allocating the bundle discount, option D recognises the whole price immediately, and option A leaves out the three months of data service.

questions.question: A Lagos company invoices a customer N2,150,000, which includes VAT at 7.5% that it collects on behalf of the tax authority. What is the transaction price under IFRS 15?
questions.explanation: The transaction price excludes amounts collected on behalf of third parties, such as VAT, so it is N2,150,000/1.075 = N2,000,000. Option C wrongly includes the VAT. Option A deducts 7.5% of the VAT-inclusive amount instead of removing the VAT element, and option D adds VAT a second time.

questions.question: Abuja Drinks Ltd sells 10,000 crates to a distributor at N1,000 per crate under a contract that entitles the distributor to a 5% rebate, which Abuja Drinks expects to pay. What is the transaction price?
questions.explanation: Rebates are among the factors that determine the transaction price, so the expected 5% rebate reduces it: N10,000,000 x 95% = N9,500,000. Option D ignores the rebate. Option C adds the rebate instead of deducting it, and option A is only the rebate amount.

questions.question: Kaduna Grains Ltd sells to a customer at N500 per bag for the year, falling to N400 per bag for all bags if the customer buys more than 2,000 bags in the year. In March the customer buys 900 bags, and Kaduna Grains does not expect the target to be met. In August the customer buys 800 more bags, and Kaduna Grains now expects the target to be met. By how much must revenue already recognised on the March sale be reduced in August?
questions.explanation: Once the target is expected to be met, all bags are priced at N400, so the March bags were over-recognised by N100 each: 900 x N100 = N90,000. Option D values the March bags at the lower price rather than computing the difference. Option A wrongly includes the August bags, which are recorded at N400 from the start, and option B ignores the change in estimate.

questions.question: Kaduna Grains Ltd sells to a customer at N500 per bag for the year, falling to N400 per bag for all bags if the customer buys more than 2,000 bags in the year. In March the customer buys 900 bags, and Kaduna Grains does not expect the target to be met. In August the customer buys 800 more bags, and Kaduna Grains now expects the target to be met. What is the net revenue Kaduna Grains recognises in August, after adjusting for the March sale?
questions.explanation: The August bags are recorded at the new price, 800 x N400 = N320,000, and the March sale is reduced by 900 x N100 = N90,000, giving net revenue of N230,000. Option D forgets the reduction on the March bags and option A still uses the old price. Option C adds the adjustment instead of deducting it.

questions.question: Kaduna Grains Ltd sells to a customer at N500 per bag for the year, falling to N400 per bag for all bags if the customer buys more than 2,000 bags in the year. In March the customer buys 900 bags, and Kaduna Grains does not expect the target to be met. In August the customer buys 800 more bags, and Kaduna Grains now expects the target to be met. In November the customer buys a further 400 bags. What is Kaduna Grains' total revenue from this customer for the year?
questions.explanation: The customer bought 2,100 bags, more than 2,000, so every bag is priced at N400: 2,100 x N400 = N840,000. Option C ignores the volume discount. Option A forgets to reduce the March bags to the lower price, and option B deducts the March adjustment twice.

questions.question: Kano Oils Ltd agrees to sell oil at N1,000 per litre, falling to N800 per litre for all litres if the customer buys more than 2,500 litres in the year. From the start, Kano Oils expects the customer to exceed 2,500 litres. In the first quarter the customer buys 1,200 litres. How much revenue is recognised for the first quarter?
questions.explanation: Because Kano Oils expects the target to be met from inception, it estimates the price as N800 per litre and recognises 1,200 x N800 = N960,000. Option D uses the full price, which applies only when the target is not expected to be met. Option C is just the discount on the litres sold, and option B recognises revenue on litres not yet delivered.

questions.question: Ondo Paints Ltd sells paint at N5,000 per bucket, falling to N4,000 per bucket for all buckets if the customer buys more than 1,000 buckets in the year. Ondo Paints never expects the target to be met, and the customer buys 700 buckets in the year. What revenue is recognised for the year?
questions.explanation: Since the target is not expected to be met and is not met, all 700 buckets are priced at N5,000: 700 x N5,000 = N3,500,000. Option A wrongly applies the volume discount price. Option B recognises revenue on the threshold quantity rather than buckets actually sold, and option C is only the discount amount.

questions.question: On 1 July 2025, Ibadan Cleaners Ltd signs a 24-month cleaning contract for N2,400,000, with the service provided evenly. How much revenue is recognised for the year ended 31 December 2025?
questions.explanation: Cleaning is a service consumed as it is performed, so revenue is recognised over time: 6/24 x N2,400,000 = N600,000. Option D recognises the whole contract at once. Option C treats half the contract as done after six months, and option B is only one month of service.

questions.question: Delta Builders Ltd has a contract, satisfied over time, to build a road for N50,000,000. Total expected costs are N40,000,000, and costs incurred to date are N12,000,000. Using costs incurred as the measure of progress, how much revenue is recognised to date?
questions.explanation: Progress is 12,000,000/40,000,000 = 30%, so revenue to date is 30% x N50,000,000 = N15,000,000. Option A is just the costs incurred, not revenue. Option D is the expected total profit, and option C is the revenue still to be recognised on the remaining 70% of the work.

questions.question: Sokoto Equipment Ltd receives a non-refundable N3,000,000 from a customer, followed later by a further N1,000,000, but the payment terms of the arrangement have still not been identified. What amount of revenue is recognised, and what is the liability?
questions.explanation: Because the payment terms are not identified, no contract exists for IFRS 15 purposes, so both the first payment and any later payments are held as a liability: N3,000,000 + N1,000,000 = N4,000,000. Option D wrongly treats the non-refundable amount as revenue, and option B recognises everything as revenue. Option C forgets that future payments are also held as a liability.

questions.question: Estimating the effect of an expected volume discount on the amount an entity will receive from a customer is part of which IFRS 15 step?
questions.explanation: A volume discount is variable consideration, and estimating it is part of determining the transaction price in Step 3. Option C comes after, when the price is shared out across performance obligations. Options B and D deal with whether a contract exists and what has been promised, not how much will be received.

questions.question: IAS 1 requires the reporting entity to prepare and present a complete set of financial statements. Which of the following is NOT a component of a complete set of financial statements under IAS 1?

options.d: Notes, comprising material accounting policy information and other explanatory information

questions.explanation: Under IAS 1, a complete set comprises the statement of financial position, the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, the statement of changes in equity, the statement of cash flows, and the notes, with comparative information. A directors' report may be required by company law, but it is outside the IAS 1 set. Options C, A and D are all required components.

questions.question: Gbojunbe Limited's trial balance at 31 December 2024 shows (N'000): Inventory at 1 January 2024 1,300; Purchases 9,062; Sales 13,040. Closing inventory at 31 December 2024 is valued at N1,600,000. Using the cost of sales method, what is the gross profit for the year?
questions.explanation: Cost of sales = opening inventory N1,300,000 + purchases N9,062,000 - closing inventory N1,600,000 = N8,762,000, so gross profit = N13,040,000 - N8,762,000 = N4,278,000. Option B forgets to deduct closing inventory, and option C leaves out opening inventory. Option A is simply sales less purchases, ignoring both inventory figures.

questions.question: Gbojunbe Limited's trial balance at 31 December 2024 includes (N'000): Inventory at 1 January 2024 1,300; Purchases 9,062; Sales 13,040; Furniture and fittings at cost 300; Irrecoverable debts 60; Insurance 69; Office expenses 115; Rates 21; General expenses 225; Rent received 119; Tax 982. Closing inventory is valued at N1,600,000 and depreciation on furniture and fittings is 10% per annum on cost. Taking rent received as other income and the tax figure as the tax charge for the year, what is the profit before tax?
questions.explanation: Gross profit is N13,040,000 - (N1,300,000 + N9,062,000 - N1,600,000) = N4,278,000; add rent received of N119,000 and deduct expenses of N60,000 + N69,000 + N115,000 + N21,000 + N225,000 + depreciation N30,000 = N520,000, giving N3,877,000. Option D is profit after deducting the N982,000 tax. Option B leaves out the rent received, and option C forgets the N30,000 depreciation.

questions.question: IAS 1 prescribes the basis for presentation of general purpose financial statements mainly to ensure

options.a: uniform tax computation between entities in the same industry
options.b: comparability with the entity's own previous periods and with other entities' financial statements
options.c: that all assets are measured at fair value at the end of each reporting period
options.d: that the statement of cash flows is prepared using the indirect method

questions.explanation: The objective of IAS 1 is comparability: users should be able to compare an entity's statements with its own earlier periods and with those of other entities. Option C is wrong because IAS 1 does not set measurement rules such as fair value for all assets. Option D relates to IAS 7, and option A is a tax matter outside IAS 1.

questions.question: IAS 1 sets out the line items to be presented in each of the following financial statements EXCEPT the

options.a: statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income

questions.explanation: IAS 1 sets out line items for each financial statement except the statement of cash flows, whose presentation and disclosure are governed by IAS 7. Options B, A and D are all statements whose minimum line items or contents are laid down in IAS 1 itself.

questions.question: IAS 1 does NOT apply to the structure and content of

options.a: annual consolidated financial statements of a group
options.b: annual separate financial statements of a parent
options.c: annual general purpose financial statements of a listed bank
options.d: condensed interim financial statements prepared under IAS 34

questions.explanation: Condensed interim financial statements take their structure and content from IAS 34 Interim Financial Reporting, so they fall outside IAS 1 on that point. IAS 1 applies equally to consolidated statements (option A), separate statements (option B) and the annual general purpose statements of any entity, including a bank (option C).

questions.question: Financial statements intended to meet the needs of users who are not in a position to require an entity to prepare reports tailored to their particular information needs are called
questions.explanation: General purpose financial statements serve users, such as investors and lenders, who cannot demand custom reports and so must rely on the published statements. Option C describes shortened mid-year statements under IAS 34, option A describes reports tailored to a particular user, and option D describes the statements of a group, which is a different idea.

questions.question: Under IAS 1, financial statements are best described as

options.a: a narrative review by management of the principal uncertainties the entity faces
options.b: a summary of the entity's budget and forecasts for the next financial year
options.c: a report on environmental matters and value added by the entity
options.d: a structured representation of the financial position and financial performance of an entity

questions.explanation: Financial statements are a structured representation of an entity's financial position and financial performance, giving information useful to a wide range of users in making economic decisions. Option A is a management financial review and option C describes environmental reports and value added statements, both presented outside the financial statements. Option B is wrong because IAS 1 does not require budgets or forecasts.

questions.question: Apart from providing information useful for economic decisions, financial statements also show

options.a: the tax liability of each individual shareholder
options.b: the market value of the entity's shares at the reporting date
options.c: the personal financial position of the entity's directors
options.d: the results of management's stewardship of the resources entrusted to it

questions.explanation: Financial statements also show how well management has looked after (stewarded) the resources that owners entrusted to it. Options B, C and A are not things IAS 1 requires financial statements to show; the share price, directors' personal finances and shareholders' own tax are outside the entity's financial statements.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of a complete set of financial statements under IAS 1?

options.a: A statement of changes in equity for the period
options.b: Notes comprising significant accounting policies and other explanatory information
options.c: A statement of cash flows for the period
options.d: A financial review by management presented outside the financial statements

questions.explanation: A management financial review is commonly published alongside the financial statements, but it sits outside them and outside the scope of IFRSs. Options A, C and B are all components of the complete set, together with the statement of financial position and the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income.

questions.question: Ikeja Paints Plc changed an accounting policy and applied it retrospectively, and the change has a material effect on its statement of financial position at the beginning of the preceding period. How many statements of financial position must it present?

options.a: Two: end of current period and end of preceding period only
options.b: Four: end of current period and the three preceding period ends
options.c: One: end of current period, with the change explained in the notes
options.d: Three: end of current period, end of preceding period and beginning of preceding period

questions.explanation: When a retrospective change in policy, retrospective restatement or reclassification has a material effect on the opening position of the preceding period, a third statement of financial position is required, giving three in total. Option A is the normal minimum without such a change, option C ignores comparatives altogether, and option B goes further than IAS 1 requires.

questions.question: An entity that chooses to present its profit or loss section in a separate statement of profit or loss must

options.a: present other comprehensive income first, followed by the profit or loss section
options.b: place it immediately after the statement of changes in equity
options.c: place it immediately before the statement presenting comprehensive income, which begins with profit or loss
options.d: present it only in the notes to the financial statements

questions.explanation: If profit or loss is shown in a separate statement, that statement must come immediately before the statement presenting comprehensive income, and that second statement starts with profit or loss. Option B breaks the required order, option D wrongly moves a primary statement into the notes to the financial statements, and option A reverses the order IAS 1 requires.

questions.question: Lekki Foods Ltd wants to title its performance statement 'statement of comprehensive income' instead of 'statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income'. Under IAS 1 this is

options.a: permitted, because an entity may use titles other than those used in IAS 1
options.b: permitted only for entities that are not-for-profit organisations
options.c: prohibited, because only the titles used in IAS 1 may be used
options.d: permitted only if the entity also presents a separate statement of profit or loss

questions.explanation: IAS 1 allows other titles for the statements, and it gives 'statement of comprehensive income' as an example. Option C is wrong because the titles are not compulsory, and options D and B add conditions that IAS 1 does not impose.

questions.question: Fair presentation under IAS 1 requires

options.a: ignoring IFRS requirements whenever management believes profit would be higher
options.b: faithful representation of the effects of transactions in line with the Conceptual Framework's definitions and recognition criteria
options.c: presenting all assets and liabilities at their market values at the reporting date
options.d: presenting the financial statements in the format preferred by the tax authority

questions.explanation: Fair presentation means faithfully representing the effects of transactions, other events and conditions using the Conceptual Framework's definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, income and expenses. Applying IFRSs, with extra disclosure when needed, is presumed to achieve it. Options C and D are not requirements of IAS 1, and option A is the opposite of fair presentation.

questions.question: An entity whose financial statements comply with IFRSs shall

options.a: obtain approval from the IASB before claiming compliance
options.b: state compliance only if it is listed on a stock exchange
options.c: describe its statements as complying with IFRSs even if a few requirements are not met
options.d: make an explicit and unreserved statement of such compliance in the notes

questions.explanation: IAS 1 requires an explicit and unreserved statement of compliance with IFRSs in the notes to the financial statements, and statements may be described as compliant only if they meet all IFRS requirements. Option C is wrong because partial compliance cannot be called compliance, and options B and A add conditions that do not exist.

questions.question: An entity shall prepare its financial statements on a going concern basis unless management

options.a: plans to raise new share capital in the next financial year
options.b: has changed the entity's reporting date during the year
options.c: intends to liquidate the entity or cease trading, or has no realistic alternative but to do so
options.d: expects the entity to make a loss in the next financial year

questions.explanation: The going concern basis is used unless management intends to liquidate or stop trading, or has no realistic alternative but to do so. A loss in the next year (option D) does not by itself end going concern, and raising capital (option A) or changing the reporting date (option B) has nothing to do with this test.

questions.question: In assessing whether the going concern assumption is appropriate, management takes into account all available information about the future covering

options.a: exactly six months from the date the financial statements are authorised
options.b: at least, but not limited to, twelve months from the end of the reporting period
options.c: only the period remaining until the next annual general meeting
options.d: no more than twelve months from the start of the reporting period

questions.explanation: Management looks at all available information about the future for at least twelve months from the end of the reporting period, and it may look further. Option A is too short and measured from the wrong date, option D wrongly caps the period and starts it at the wrong point, and option C is not a period IAS 1 uses.

questions.question: The shareholders of Agege Bakeries Ltd have resolved to wind up the company soon after the year end, so the statements are not prepared on a going concern basis. IAS 1 requires the company to disclose

options.a: only a forecast of the cash expected from selling its assets
options.b: nothing, since the company will soon cease to exist
options.c: that fact, the basis on which it prepared the statements and the reason it is not regarded as a going concern
options.d: only the names of the liquidators appointed

questions.explanation: When statements are not prepared on a going concern basis, the entity must disclose that fact, the basis used instead and why it is not a going concern. Option B ignores this requirement, and options D and A are not the disclosures IAS 1 requires; IAS 1 does not require forecasts.

questions.question: Surulere Prints Ltd delivered goods worth N4 million to a customer in December 2025 (year end 31 December 2025), but the customer paid in February 2026. Recognising the sale in 2025 is an application of which IAS 1 general feature?
questions.explanation: Under the accrual basis, items are recognised when they meet the definitions and recognition criteria, not when cash moves, so the sale belongs to 2025. Option D concerns netting assets with liabilities or income with expenses, option C concerns how often statements are presented, and option B concerns keeping the same presentation from year to year.

questions.question: Information whose omission, misstatement or obscuring could reasonably be expected to influence the decisions primary users make on the basis of general purpose financial statements is described as
questions.explanation: This is the IAS 1 definition of material information. Option D means a requirement cannot be applied after every reasonable effort, option C is a quality of information that allows comparison, and option B describes combining items into classes; none of these is the test of influence on decisions.

questions.question: Under IAS 1, materiality depends on

options.a: the magnitude of the item only, measured against revenue
options.b: the preferences of the entity's directors only
options.c: the nature or magnitude of information, or both
options.d: whether the item has been audited

questions.explanation: Materiality depends on the nature of the information, its size, or both, judged in the context of the financial statements as a whole. Option A is too narrow because a small item can be material by nature, while options D and B are not bases IAS 1 uses.

questions.question: An item that is not individually material enough to warrant separate presentation in the financial statements

options.a: must always be omitted from both the statements and the notes
options.b: is aggregated with other items, and may still warrant separate presentation in the notes
options.c: must be offset against a related liability
options.d: must be presented as an extraordinary item

questions.explanation: A line item that is not individually material is aggregated with other items, and it may still deserve separate presentation in the notes to the financial statements. Option A is wrong because aggregation does not mean leaving it out, option C confuses materiality with offsetting, and option D is wrong because extraordinary items are prohibited.

questions.question: IAS 1 states that an entity shall not offset assets and liabilities, or income and expenses,

options.a: unless required or permitted by an IFRS
options.c: unless the amounts involved are material

questions.explanation: Offsetting is not allowed unless an IFRS requires or permits it, because netting can hide the transactions and make future cash flows harder to assess. Option C gets materiality the wrong way round, option B is not a valid ground, and option D is too absolute, since some IFRSs do require or permit offsetting.

questions.question: Kano Textiles Ltd has many small foreign exchange gains and losses arising from a group of similar transactions. Under IAS 1 these are normally presented

options.a: on a net basis, but separately if they are material
options.b: gross, with every gain and every loss on a separate line
options.d: directly in retained earnings, bypassing profit or loss

questions.explanation: Gains and losses from a group of similar transactions, such as foreign exchange gains and losses, are presented net, but shown separately if they are material. Option B is not required for a group of similar items, and options C and D take ordinary foreign exchange differences out of profit or loss without any basis.

questions.question: An entity changes its reporting date and presents financial statements for an 18-month period. In addition to the period covered, IAS 1 requires disclosure of

options.a: the reason for the longer period and the fact that the amounts are not entirely comparable
options.b: a restated 12-month version of every statement
options.c: the approval of the tax authority for the change
options.d: nothing further, provided the statements are audited

questions.explanation: A complete set must be presented at least annually, and when the period is longer or shorter than a year the entity discloses why and that the amounts are not entirely comparable. Option D ignores the requirement, while options B and C are not what IAS 1 asks for.

questions.question: As a minimum, IAS 1 requires an entity to present

options.a: three of each statement for every reporting period
options.b: one of each statement, with comparatives shown only in the notes
options.c: two statements of financial position but only one of each other statement
options.d: two statements of financial position, two statements of profit or loss and OCI, two statements of cash flows and two statements of changes in equity, with related notes

questions.explanation: Comparative information for the preceding period is required for all amounts, so the minimum is two of each statement (current and prior period) plus related notes. Option B leaves out the comparative statements, option A goes beyond the minimum, and option C wrongly limits comparatives to the statement of financial position.

questions.question: Ibadan Ceramics Ltd moved 'delivery costs' from administrative expenses to distribution costs this year. Under IAS 1 it should

options.a: present the change as an extraordinary item
options.b: reclassify the comparative amounts, unless reclassification is impracticable, and disclose the nature, amount and reason
options.c: present the change as a prior period error in the statement of changes in equity
options.d: leave the comparatives unchanged and say nothing

questions.explanation: When presentation or classification changes, comparative amounts are reclassified unless that is impracticable, with disclosure of the nature, the amounts and the reason. Option D damages comparability, option C wrongly treats a reclassification as an error, and option A is not allowed because extraordinary items are prohibited.

questions.question: Under the consistency of presentation requirement, an entity may change the presentation or classification of items from one period to the next when

options.a: a significant change in the nature of its operations makes another presentation more appropriate, or an IFRS requires a change
options.b: a new finance director prefers a different format
options.c: the new presentation shows a higher profit
options.d: the entity wants to make comparison with the prior year harder

questions.explanation: Presentation and classification are kept from period to period unless a significant change in operations (or a review) shows that another presentation is more appropriate, or an IFRS requires a change. Options B, C and D are personal or self-serving reasons that would damage comparability.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a line item IAS 1 requires to be presented in the statement of financial position?
questions.explanation: Cost of sales is an expense line found in the statement of profit or loss under the function of expense method, not in the statement of financial position. Options D, B and A are all listed among the minimum line items of the statement of financial position.

questions.question: When an entity uses the current/non-current classification in its statement of financial position, deferred tax assets and liabilities shall be classified as

options.a: current or non-current depending on when they reverse

questions.explanation: IAS 1 does not allow deferred tax assets or liabilities to be classified as current when the current/non-current split is used, so they appear as non-current. Option B is prohibited, option A is a timing test IAS 1 does not apply to deferred tax, and option C is wrong because deferred tax is not equity.

questions.question: IAS 1 permits an entity to present all assets and liabilities in order of liquidity, instead of a current/non-current split, when

options.a: the entity wishes to hide its long-term debt
options.b: the entity has more current assets than non-current assets
options.c: a liquidity presentation provides information that is reliable and more relevant, as for many financial institutions
options.d: the entity has made a loss for the year

questions.explanation: The current/non-current split is the normal approach, but a liquidity-based presentation is used when it gives reliable and more relevant information, for example for financial institutions without a clearly identifiable operating cycle. Options B, A and D are not grounds IAS 1 recognises.

questions.question: An asset is classified as current under IAS 1 when any of the following applies, EXCEPT when

options.a: the entity intends to use it to generate income over several years
options.b: it is held primarily for the purpose of trading
options.c: the entity expects to realise it, or intends to sell or consume it, in its normal operating cycle
options.d: the entity expects to realise it within twelve months after the reporting period

questions.explanation: An asset used to earn income over several years, such as a factory machine, fails all four current-asset tests and is non-current. Options C, B and D are three of the criteria for a current asset; the fourth is cash or cash equivalents that are not restricted.

questions.question: Onitsha Spirits Ltd matures whisky for three years before sale, as part of its normal operating cycle. At the reporting date, how should this maturing inventory be classified?

options.a: As a non-current asset until the final year of maturing
options.b: As investment property, because it is held for capital appreciation
options.c: As a non-current asset, because it will not be sold within twelve months
options.d: As a current asset, because it will be realised in the entity's normal operating cycle

questions.explanation: Assets sold, consumed or realised as part of the normal operating cycle are current even when they will not be realised within twelve months after the reporting period. Options C and A wrongly apply only the twelve-month test, and option B is wrong because inventory is not investment property.

questions.question: When an entity's normal operating cycle is not clearly identifiable, IAS 1 assumes it to be

options.a: the period until the next annual general meeting
options.c: the life of the entity's longest-lived asset

questions.explanation: The operating cycle is the time from acquiring assets for processing until they are realised in cash, and when it cannot be clearly identified it is assumed to be twelve months. Options D, C and A are not periods IAS 1 uses.

questions.question: A liability is classified as current under IAS 1 when any of the following applies, EXCEPT when

options.a: management merely intends to repay it early, although the entity has the right to defer settlement for at least twelve months
options.b: the entity expects to settle it in its normal operating cycle
options.c: it is held primarily for the purpose of trading
options.d: it is due to be settled within twelve months after the reporting period

questions.explanation: Classification is unaffected by management's intention or expectation to settle early; if the entity has the right at the reporting date to defer settlement for at least twelve months, the liability stays non-current. Options B, C and D are three of the four criteria for a current liability.

questions.question: Port Harcourt Oil Services Ltd has trade payables that are part of its normal operating cycle but are due 14 months after the reporting date. They should be classified as

options.a: current liabilities, because they are part of the working capital used in the normal operating cycle
options.b: non-current liabilities, because they are due after more than twelve months
options.c: contingent liabilities disclosed only in the notes
options.d: equity, because they are not yet due

questions.explanation: Operating items such as trade payables are current liabilities even if they are due more than twelve months after the reporting period, because they form part of working capital in the normal operating cycle. Option B applies only the twelve-month test, and options D and C are wrong because trade payables are present obligations recognised as liabilities.

questions.question: Abuja Cement Plc has a bank loan due for repayment four months after its reporting date of 31 December 2025. On 20 February 2026, before the statements are authorised for issue, the bank agrees to refinance it on a long-term basis. At 31 December 2025 the loan is

options.a: split equally between current and non-current liabilities
options.b: a current liability, with the refinancing disclosed as a non-adjusting event
options.c: removed from the statement of financial position
options.d: a non-current liability, because it has been refinanced long-term

questions.explanation: A financial liability due within twelve months is current even if a long-term refinancing is agreed after the reporting period but before authorisation; at the reporting date the entity had no right to defer settlement. Option D wrongly uses an event after the reporting period to change the classification, option A has no basis, and option C is wrong because the debt still exists.

questions.question: Benin Rubber Ltd breached a covenant on its long-term loan before its year end, making the loan payable on demand. After the year end, but before the statements were authorised, the lender agreed not to demand payment. At the reporting date the loan is

options.b: a non-current liability, because the lender later waived the breach
options.c: a contingent liability disclosed only in the notes
options.d: part of equity until the breach is rectified

questions.explanation: Because the breach made the loan payable on demand and, at the reporting date, the entity had no right to defer settlement for twelve months, the loan is current, even though the lender agreed after the year end not to demand payment. Option B wrongly relies on the later waiver, and options C and D misdescribe a recognised loan.

questions.question: Calabar Fisheries Ltd breached a loan covenant, but by its year end the lender had agreed a grace period ending 15 months after the reporting date, during which the lender cannot demand repayment. The loan should be classified as

options.a: current, until the breach is actually rectified
options.b: current, because a breach occurred during the year

questions.explanation: If the lender agrees, by the end of the reporting period, to a grace period ending at least twelve months after the reporting date, during which it cannot demand repayment, the liability is non-current. Options B and A would apply only if no such grace period existed at the reporting date, and option D is wrong because a loan is a liability.

questions.question: In addition to the profit or loss and other comprehensive income sections, the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income shall present

options.a: profit or loss, total other comprehensive income and comprehensive income for the period
options.d: only revenue and profit before tax

questions.explanation: The statement must show profit or loss, total other comprehensive income, and comprehensive income for the period (the total of the two). Option D is incomplete, option B belongs in the statement of changes in equity, and option C belongs in the statement of cash flows.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a line item required in the profit or loss section of the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income?

options.c: A single amount for the total of discontinued operations

questions.explanation: Changes in revaluation surplus are a component of other comprehensive income, not of profit or loss. Options A, D and C are all minimum line items of the profit or loss section.

questions.question: Ilorin Hotels Ltd revalued its hotel building upwards by N30 million under the IAS 16 revaluation model. The revaluation gain is recognised in

options.b: profit or loss, as other income
options.d: the statement of cash flows as an investing inflow

questions.explanation: Changes in revaluation surplus under IAS 16 are a component of other comprehensive income. Options B and A wrongly put an unrealised revaluation gain in profit or loss, and option D is wrong because no cash has been received.

questions.question: Which of the following items is recognised in profit or loss rather than in other comprehensive income?

options.a: An impairment loss on trade receivables under IFRS 9
options.b: A remeasurement of a defined benefit pension plan
options.c: A gain on translating the financial statements of a foreign operation
options.d: A gain on an equity investment designated at fair value through OCI

questions.explanation: Impairment losses (and their reversals) determined under IFRS 9 are a required line item in the profit or loss section. Options B, C and D are all listed components of other comprehensive income.

questions.question: Which of the following is a component of other comprehensive income?

options.a: A gain on the disposal of a delivery van
options.b: Interest revenue calculated using the effective interest method
options.c: The share of the profit of an associate accounted for using the equity method
options.d: The effective portion of gains and losses on hedging instruments in a cash flow hedge

questions.explanation: The effective portion of gains and losses on hedging instruments in a cash flow hedge is listed as a component of OCI. Option A is a disposal gain reported in profit or loss, while options B and C are required line items of the profit or loss section.

questions.question: Nigerian company Zaria Holdings Plc translates the financial statements of its Ghanaian subsidiary into naira and makes a translation loss. This loss is reported in other comprehensive income as an item that

options.a: is reported as an extraordinary item
options.b: will be reclassified subsequently to profit or loss when specific conditions are met, such as disposal of the foreign operation
options.c: is transferred directly to retained earnings each year
options.d: will never be reclassified subsequently to profit or loss

questions.explanation: Gains and losses from translating a foreign operation are OCI items that are reclassified to profit or loss when specific conditions are met, for example when the foreign operation is disposed of. Option D describes items such as revaluation surplus and defined benefit remeasurements, option C has no basis, and option A is prohibited.

questions.question: Which pair of OCI items will NOT be reclassified subsequently to profit or loss?

options.a: Foreign operation translation differences and cash flow hedge gains
options.b: Remeasurements of defined benefit plans and cash flow hedge gains
options.c: Revaluation surplus changes and foreign operation translation differences
options.d: Changes in revaluation surplus and remeasurements of defined benefit plans

questions.explanation: Reclassification adjustments do not arise on changes in revaluation surplus or on remeasurements of defined benefit plans; these stay out of profit or loss (revaluation surplus may be moved to retained earnings instead). Options A, C and B each include at least one item, foreign translation differences or cash flow hedge gains, that can be reclassified to profit or loss.

questions.question: Amounts reclassified to profit or loss in the current period that were recognised in other comprehensive income in the current or previous periods are called
questions.explanation: Reclassification adjustments move amounts previously recognised in OCI into profit or loss, so that they are not counted twice in total comprehensive income. Options C and D relate to IAS 8 corrections of earlier periods, and option A covers items such as dividends and share issues.

questions.question: IAS 1 states that items of income or expense may be presented as extraordinary items

options.a: only in the other comprehensive income section
options.b: only in the notes to the financial statements
options.c: only when they are both unusual and material
options.d: in neither the statements presenting profit or loss and OCI nor the notes

questions.explanation: IAS 1 bans the presentation of any item of income or expense as extraordinary, whether in the statements or in the notes to the financial statements. Options B, C and A each suggest a place or condition where extraordinary items would be allowed, and there is none.

questions.question: Total comprehensive income is the change in equity during a period resulting from transactions and other events, other than

options.a: changes resulting from foreign currency translation
options.b: changes resulting from transactions with owners in their capacity as owners
options.c: changes resulting from the sale of inventory
options.d: changes resulting from revaluation of property

questions.explanation: Total comprehensive income covers all income and expense, both profit or loss and OCI, and excludes only owner changes such as share issues and dividends. Options D and A are OCI items and option C gives rise to profit or loss, so all three are part of total comprehensive income.

questions.question: Which of the following line items appears in a statement of profit or loss prepared using the nature of expense method?

options.b: Changes in inventories of finished goods and work in progress

questions.explanation: The nature of expense method groups expenses by their nature, such as changes in inventories, raw materials used, employee benefits and depreciation. Cost of sales (option D), distribution costs (option C) and gross profit (option A) belong to the function of expense (cost of sales) method.

questions.question: An entity that classifies expenses by function is required to disclose additional information on the nature of expenses, including

options.a: the expected cash flows for the next five years
options.b: the market value of its shares
options.c: depreciation and amortisation expense and employee benefits expense
options.d: the names of its main suppliers

questions.explanation: Because information on the nature of expenses helps users predict future cash flows, entities using the function method must also disclose depreciation and amortisation and employee benefits expense. Options A, B and D are not disclosures required by this rule; IAS 1 does not require forecasts.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares the two methods of analysing expenses?

options.a: The function method is simple because no allocation is needed, while the nature method needs arbitrary allocations
options.b: Both methods require expenses to be allocated to functions
options.c: IAS 1 requires all entities to use the nature method
options.d: The nature method is simple because no allocation to functions is needed, while the function method can be more relevant but may need arbitrary allocations

questions.explanation: Under the nature method, expenses are not reallocated among functions, which makes it simple to apply; the function method can give more relevant information but allocating costs may involve arbitrary choices and judgement. Option A reverses the two methods, option B is wrong for the nature method, and option C is wrong because management chooses whichever is reliable and more relevant.

questions.question: The statement of changes in equity is described as linking which two statements?

options.a: The statement of financial position and the statement of comprehensive income
options.b: The statement of comprehensive income and the statement of cash flows
options.c: The statement of cash flows and the notes
options.d: The statement of financial position and the statement of cash flows

questions.explanation: The statement of changes in equity carries total comprehensive income for the period into the equity balances shown in the statement of financial position, so it links those two statements. Options C, D and B pair statements that the statement of changes in equity does not connect in this way.

questions.question: For each component of equity, the statement of changes in equity reconciles opening and closing carrying amounts, separately disclosing changes resulting from

options.a: profit or loss, other comprehensive income and transactions with owners in their capacity as owners
options.b: current assets, non-current assets and liabilities
options.d: revenue, cost of sales and administrative expenses

questions.explanation: The reconciliation for each component of equity shows, as a minimum, changes from profit or loss, from other comprehensive income and from transactions with owners as owners. Option C is the classification used in the statement of cash flows, option B relates to the statement of financial position, and option D lists profit or loss line items.

questions.question: In the statement of changes in equity, which of the following is a transaction with owners in their capacity as owners?

options.c: Payment of a dividend to ordinary shareholders
options.d: A remeasurement loss on a defined benefit plan

questions.explanation: Dividends paid are distributions to owners in their capacity as owners, as are share issues. Option A and option D are OCI items and option B is profit or loss, so all three form part of total comprehensive income rather than owner transactions.

questions.question: The amount of dividends recognised as distributions to owners during the period, and the related dividends per share, shall be presented

options.a: in the other comprehensive income section
options.b: in the profit or loss section as an expense
options.c: either in the statement of changes in equity or in the notes
options.d: only in the directors' report outside the financial statements

questions.explanation: Dividends recognised as distributions, and dividends per share, go in the statement of changes in equity or the notes to the financial statements, because they are owner transactions and not expenses. Options B and A wrongly treat dividends as part of comprehensive income, and option D puts required information outside the financial statements.

questions.question: Under IAS 1, the statement of cash flows provides information about

options.b: the entity's assets and liabilities at the reporting date
options.c: the ability of the entity to generate cash and cash equivalents and its needs to utilise those cash flows
options.d: changes in each component of equity during the period

questions.explanation: Cash flow information shows users the entity's ability to generate cash and cash equivalents and its needs to use them, with detailed rules in IAS 7. Option D describes the statement of changes in equity, option A the notes to the financial statements, and option B the statement of financial position.

questions.question: Which of the following is a function of the notes to the financial statements under IAS 1?

options.a: Presenting management's forecast profit for the next year
options.b: Disclosing information required by IFRSs that is not presented elsewhere in the financial statements
options.c: Correcting inappropriate accounting policies through explanation
options.d: Replacing the statement of financial position where line items are numerous

questions.explanation: The notes present the basis of preparation and accounting policies, give information required by IFRSs that is not presented elsewhere, and provide other information relevant to understanding the statements. Option D is wrong because notes support the statements and do not replace them, option C is ruled out because disclosure cannot fix bad policies, and option A is not required.

questions.question: When the notes follow the order of the line items in the statements, which of the following normally comes FIRST?

options.a: Supporting information for items presented in the statements
options.d: Summary of significant accounting policies applied

questions.explanation: The usual order starts with the statement of compliance with IFRSs, then the significant accounting policies, then supporting information for line items, then other disclosures such as contingent liabilities. Options D, A and B come second, third and fourth in that order.

questions.question: Which of the following circumstances would give rise to separate disclosure of the nature and amount of an item of income or expense, if material?

options.b: A write-down of inventories to net realisable value
options.c: Routine monthly payment of electricity bills

questions.explanation: IAS 1 lists write-downs of inventories to net realisable value as a circumstance giving rise to separate disclosure, along with restructurings, disposals of property, plant and equipment, litigation settlements and similar items. Options C, A and D are ordinary recurring transactions that are not on that list.

questions.question: Okene Foods Plc reports profit for the year of N45 million. During the year it recognised a revaluation gain on land of N8 million and a loss of N3 million on translating a foreign operation. What is total comprehensive income for the year?
questions.explanation: Total comprehensive income is profit or loss plus other comprehensive income: N45m + N8m - N3m = N50m. Option B leaves out the translation loss, option D adds the loss as if it were a gain, and option C is profit alone without any OCI.

questions.question: Gombe Agro Ltd reports total comprehensive income of N72 million, which includes other comprehensive income of N12 million. What is its profit for the year?
questions.explanation: Profit or loss is total comprehensive income less other comprehensive income: N72m - N12m = N60m. Option C adds OCI instead of deducting it, option A treats total comprehensive income as profit, and option D is OCI alone.

questions.question: Asaba Hotels Ltd recognises a revaluation gain of N10 million on its building, with related deferred tax at 30%. If it presents OCI items net of related tax effects, what amount appears for this item in OCI?
questions.explanation: Presenting net of tax means showing the gain after deducting its tax: N10m x (1 - 0.30) = N7m. Option D is the before-tax amount, option B is only the tax, and option C wrongly adds the tax to the gain.

questions.question: A Lagos-based group has total comprehensive income of N60 million, of which N12 million is attributable to non-controlling interests. How much total comprehensive income is attributable to owners of the parent?
questions.explanation: Total comprehensive income is split between owners of the parent and non-controlling interests, so the parent's share is N60m - N12m = N48m. Option B ignores the NCI share, option C adds it, and option A is the NCI share itself.

questions.question: Ota Packaging Ltd had opening retained earnings of N120 million. Profit for the year was N35 million, dividends paid were N12 million and N5 million was transferred to general reserve. What is closing retained earnings in the statement of changes in equity?
questions.explanation: Retained earnings increase by profit and decrease by dividends and the transfer to general reserve: N120m + N35m - N12m - N5m = N138m. Option A forgets the transfer, option B adds the transfer instead of deducting it, and option C ignores both the dividends and the transfer.

questions.question: Ijebu Steel Plc had opening share premium of N4 million. During the year it issued 2,000,000 ordinary shares of N1 each at N1.50 per share. What is the closing share premium?
questions.explanation: Share premium rises by the excess of the issue price over par value: 2,000,000 x (N1.50 - N1) = N1m, so the closing balance is N4m + N1m = N5m. Option A adds the whole proceeds, option B adds the par value that belongs to share capital, and option D leaves out the opening balance.

questions.question: Enugu Coal Ltd had total equity of N250 million at the start of the year. Total comprehensive income was N40 million, new shares were issued for N15 million and dividends of N10 million were paid. What is total equity at the end of the year?
questions.explanation: Closing equity is opening equity plus total comprehensive income plus owner contributions less owner distributions: N250m + N40m + N15m - N10m = N295m. Option C leaves out the share issue, option B leaves out the dividend, and option D adds the dividend instead of deducting it.

questions.question: Opening retained earnings of Lokoja Mills Ltd were N80 million before correcting a prior period error that overstated profits by N6 million. Profit for the current year is N20 million and dividends paid are N10 million. What is closing retained earnings?
questions.explanation: The error correction adjusts opening retained earnings to N74m (N80m - N6m); adding profit of N20m and deducting dividends of N10m gives N84m. Option D ignores the restatement, option B adds the overstatement instead of removing it, and option C forgets the dividends.

questions.question: At 31 December 2025, Kaduna Textiles Ltd has a bank loan of N50 million repayable in five equal annual instalments, the first due on 30 June 2026. The entity has no right to defer any instalment. How much of the loan is a non-current liability?
questions.explanation: The instalment due within twelve months (N10m) is current; the remaining N40m is due after more than twelve months and is non-current. Option A ignores the current portion, option B is the current portion, and option C wrongly treats the whole loan as current.

questions.question: Sokoto Grains Ltd has: inventories N18m, trade receivables N12m, unrestricted cash N7m, cash restricted by a court order for three years N5m, plant N60m and investment property N25m. What are its total current assets?
questions.explanation: Current assets are inventories, receivables and unrestricted cash: N18m + N12m + N7m = N37m. Cash restricted for at least twelve months is non-current, so option A wrongly includes it; option D also includes investment property, which is long-term, and option B leaves out the unrestricted cash.

questions.question: Warri Marine Ltd has: trade payables N22m, bank overdraft N6m, current tax payable N9m, a long-term loan of N40m not due within twelve months, and the current portion of another loan N8m. What are its total current liabilities?
questions.explanation: Trade payables, bank overdrafts, current tax and the current portion of loans are all current: N22m + N6m + N9m + N8m = N45m. Option A leaves out the current portion of the loan, option B wrongly adds the long-term loan, and option D leaves out the overdraft.

questions.question: Under the function of expense method, Akure Furniture Ltd reports revenue of N150 million and cost of sales of N90 million. Distribution costs are N15 million. What is gross profit?
questions.explanation: Gross profit is revenue less cost of sales: N150m - N90m = N60m. Option B also deducts distribution costs, which come after gross profit, option A is revenue alone, and option D adds cost of sales instead of deducting it.

questions.question: Using the function of expense method, Minna Plastics Ltd has: revenue N200m, cost of sales N120m, other income N5m, distribution costs N18m, administrative expenses N22m and other expenses N4m. What is profit before tax?
questions.explanation: Profit before tax = N200m - N120m + N5m - N18m - N22m - N4m = N41m. Option C deducts other income instead of adding it, option B stops at gross profit, and option A leaves out other expenses.

questions.question: Using the nature of expense method, Jos Dairies Ltd has: revenue N300m, other income N10m, an increase in inventories of finished goods and work in progress of N12m, raw materials and consumables used N140m, employee benefits expense N60m, depreciation N25m and other expenses N20m. What is profit before tax?
questions.explanation: An increase in inventories of finished goods and work in progress reduces total expenses, so total expenses = -N12m + N140m + N60m + N25m + N20m = N233m and profit before tax = N300m + N10m - N233m = N77m. Option D treats the inventory increase as an extra expense, option A leaves out other income, and option C leaves out depreciation.

questions.question: Bauchi Haulage Ltd sold a truck for N12 million. The truck's carrying amount was N9 million and selling expenses were N0.5 million. Under IAS 1's netting rule for disposals, what gain is presented?
questions.explanation: Gains on disposal of non-current assets are shown net: proceeds less carrying amount less related selling expenses, N12m - N9m - N0.5m = N2.5m. Option D ignores selling expenses, option A presents the gross proceeds, and option C ignores the carrying amount.

questions.question: Yola Distributors Ltd has gross trade receivables of N30 million and an allowance for doubtful debts of N2 million. What amount is presented for trade receivables in the statement of financial position?
questions.explanation: Receivables are measured net of the valuation allowance, N30m - N2m = N28m, and IAS 1 says this is not offsetting. Option A ignores the allowance, option C adds it, and option B is the allowance alone.

questions.question: During the year, Nnewi Motors Plc recognised a translation gain of N1 million on its foreign subsidiary and then sold the subsidiary, reclassifying cumulative translation gains of N4 million to profit or loss. What is the net amount shown for this item in OCI for the year?
questions.explanation: The N4m reclassification adjustment is deducted from OCI in the year it moves into profit or loss, so that it is not counted twice in total comprehensive income: N1m - N4m = a net loss of N3m. Option B adds the reclassification instead of deducting it, option C ignores it, and option A shows only the reclassified amount as a gain.

questions.question: Ogbomoso Farms Ltd has property, plant and equipment of N80m, inventory of N15m, trade and other receivables of N10m and cash and cash equivalents of N5m. Its share capital is N50m. What is the total assets figure in its statement of financial position?
questions.explanation: Total assets are non-current assets plus current assets: N80m + (N15m + N10m + N5m) = N110m. Option A is current assets only, while options C and D wrongly deduct or add share capital, which is part of equity and liabilities, not assets.

questions.question: Kebbi Rice Plc's OCI for the year comprises: revaluation gain on land N6m, remeasurement loss on its defined benefit plan N2m, gain on translating a foreign operation N3m and a loss on the effective portion of a cash flow hedge N1m. What total is presented for items that will NOT be reclassified subsequently to profit or loss?
questions.explanation: Revaluation surplus changes and defined benefit remeasurements are never reclassified to profit or loss, so that group totals N6m - N2m = N4m. Option A is the group that may be reclassified (translation and cash flow hedge items), option D is total OCI for the year, and option B adds the remeasurement loss as if it were a gain.

questions.question: The initial cost of an inventory is N10,000 and its net realisable value is N8,000. What is the written-down value of the inventory?
questions.explanation: IAS 2 measures inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Here NRV of N8,000 is below cost of N10,000, so the inventory is written down to N8,000 and a N2,000 loss is expensed. Option B ignores the fall in value, option C is the size of the write-down rather than the carrying value, and option A adds the two figures.

questions.question: When is a building treated as inventory?

options.b: When it is used by the entity as its head office
options.c: When it is held for sale in the ordinary course of business, for example by a property developer
options.d: When it is held to earn rental income

questions.explanation: Inventories are assets held for sale in the ordinary course of business, so a building built or bought by a property developer to sell is inventory under IAS 2. Option B describes owner-occupied property, which is property, plant and equipment under IAS 16. Option D is investment property, and option A is irrelevant because classification depends on purpose, not size.

questions.question: Power Holding Nigeria Limited's inventory records for the year ended December 2024: January opening balance 2,000 units at N2.00; February purchases 1,500 units at N2.50; March purchases 2,500 units at N3.00; April issues 2,500 units; May issues 1,000 units; June purchases 1,200 units at N3.50; July issues 1,500 units; August issues 1,200 units. The company uses FIFO. The closing inventory has an estimated sales value of N5,500 with costs to sell of N1,000. At what amount should closing inventory be measured under IAS 2?
questions.explanation: Under FIFO the oldest units go out first, so the 1,000 units left are all from the June batch at N3.50, a cost of N3,500. NRV is N5,500 - N1,000 = N4,500, and IAS 2 takes the lower of cost and NRV, which is N3,500. Option C is the NRV, which is higher than cost here. Option A ignores the costs to sell, and option D prices the units at the March cost of N3.00.

questions.question: Power Holding Nigeria Limited's inventory records for the year ended December 2024: January opening balance 2,000 units at N2.00; February purchases 1,500 units at N2.50; March purchases 2,500 units at N3.00; April issues 2,500 units; May issues 1,000 units; June purchases 1,200 units at N3.50; July issues 1,500 units; August issues 1,200 units. The company uses FIFO. The closing inventory has an estimated sales value of N5,500 with costs to sell of N1,000. Total revenue is N50,000 and operating expenses are N7,000. What is the profit before tax?
questions.explanation: Purchases total N3,750 + N7,500 + N4,200 = N15,450, so cost of sales = opening N4,000 + N15,450 - closing N3,500 (FIFO cost, below NRV of N4,500) = N15,950. Gross profit is N50,000 - N15,950 = N34,050, and after operating expenses of N7,000 profit before tax is N27,050. Option B is profit after 24% tax (N6,492). Option C values closing inventory at NRV of N4,500, and option A uses a closing inventory of N2,500.

questions.question: IAS 2 focuses on...
questions.explanation: IAS 2 is the standard on inventories, setting out how the cost of inventory is measured and when it is written down to net realisable value. Option A is IAS 23 (borrowing costs), option B relates to leases (IFRS 16, formerly IAS 17) and option D is IFRS 3 (business combinations).

questions.question: In recognising the cost of inventory to be recognised in the income statement, one of the following inventory valuation methods is not allowed by IAS 2
questions.explanation: IAS 2 does not allow the LIFO (last-in, first-out) cost formula; inventory cost must be assigned using FIFO or the weighted average cost formula (or specific identification for items that are not interchangeable). Options B and C are both permitted methods, so they are wrong. Option D is wrong because FIFO is allowed.

questions.question: Assets held for sale in the ordinary course of business, in the process of production for such sale, or in the form of materials or supplies to be consumed in the production process or in the rendering of services are called
