questions.explanation: This is the IAS 2 definition of inventories: goods held for sale, work in progress, and materials or supplies used in production or in rendering services. Option B describes assets held for use in production or supply over more than one period, not for sale. Option A is property held to earn rentals or for capital appreciation, and option C refers to living animals or plants covered by IAS 41.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three categories in the IAS 2 definition of inventories?

options.a: Assets held for use in the supply of goods over more than one period
options.b: Assets held for sale in the ordinary course of business
options.c: Materials or supplies to be consumed in the production process
options.d: Assets in the process of production for sale

questions.explanation: Holding an asset for use over more than one period describes property, plant and equipment under IAS 16, not inventories. Options B, D and C are exactly the three limbs of the inventories definition: finished goods for sale, work in progress, and materials or supplies.

questions.question: Ikeja Motors Ltd, a car dealer, holds 40 new vehicles in its showroom for sale to customers and 3 vehicles used by its sales staff for daily operations. How should the 40 showroom vehicles be classified?

options.b: As property, plant and equipment under IAS 16

questions.explanation: The 40 showroom vehicles are held for sale in the ordinary course of the dealer's business, so they are inventories. Option B would fit only the 3 vehicles the staff use in operations, not the ones held for sale. Options D and C do not apply because the cars are neither held for rental or capital appreciation nor without physical substance.

questions.question: Which of the following is excluded from the scope of IAS 2?

options.a: Work in progress of a furniture maker
options.b: Biological assets related to agricultural activity
options.c: Raw materials held by a manufacturer
options.d: Finished goods held by a retailer

questions.explanation: Biological assets related to agricultural activity, and agricultural produce at the point of harvest, are dealt with by IAS 41 Agriculture, so they fall outside IAS 2. Options C, D and A are ordinary raw materials, finished goods and work in progress, which are the typical inventories IAS 2 covers.

questions.question: Which of the following items is excluded from the scope of IAS 2 Inventories?

options.a: Goods purchased and held for resale
options.b: Partly finished goods in a factory
options.d: Spare parts and consumable supplies held for production

questions.explanation: Financial instruments are excluded from IAS 2 because they are covered by the standards on financial instruments. Option D is materials or supplies to be consumed in production, option A is goods held for sale, and option B is work in progress, so all three are inventories within IAS 2.

questions.question: Under IAS 2, inventories shall be measured at

options.b: Fair value less costs to sell
options.c: The higher of cost and net realisable value
options.d: The lower of cost and net realisable value

questions.explanation: IAS 2 requires inventories to be measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value, so they are never carried above the amount expected to be recovered from sale. Option C would overstate assets, option B is the basis used for certain items such as biological assets rather than general inventories, and option A applies to depreciable assets like property, plant and equipment.

questions.question: The estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business less the estimated costs of completion and the estimated costs necessary to make the sale is called
questions.explanation: This is the definition of net realisable value, which is entity-specific and looks at what the entity itself expects to recover from selling the item. Option B is a market-based exit price between participants, not reduced by completion costs. Option D is the current cost of buying the item again, and option A is the cost of turning materials into finished goods.

questions.question: Which of the following is deducted from the estimated selling price in arriving at net realisable value?

options.b: Estimated costs of completion and estimated costs necessary to make the sale
options.d: Original purchase price and import duties

questions.explanation: Net realisable value equals estimated selling price less the estimated costs to complete the item and the estimated costs needed to sell it. Option D lists elements of cost, which is compared with NRV rather than deducted from selling price. Options A and C are not part of the NRV formula at all.

questions.question: Oshodi Textiles Ltd holds a batch of fabric that cost N500,000. It is expected to sell for N480,000 after further finishing costing N30,000, and selling costs of N20,000 will be incurred. What write-down is required under IAS 2?
questions.explanation: Net realisable value is N480,000 - N30,000 - N20,000 = N430,000, which is below cost of N500,000, so the batch is written down by N70,000. Option C compares cost with the selling price only and ignores the deductions. Option A deducts only one of the two costs, and option B wrongly assumes no write-down is needed.

questions.question: Yaba Electronics Ltd has a stock of 200 phone chargers costing N3,000 each. Each can be sold for N3,200, but packaging and delivery costs of N400 per unit will be incurred to sell them. At what amount should the chargers be reported in the statement of financial position?
questions.explanation: NRV per unit is N3,200 - N400 = N2,800, which is below cost of N3,000, so the chargers are carried at 200 x N2,800 = N560,000. Option C is cost, which is higher than NRV here. Option D uses the gross selling price without deducting selling costs, and option B deducts the selling costs twice.

questions.question: Surulere Stores Ltd holds three unrelated product lines at year end. Line A: cost N200,000, NRV N260,000. Line B: cost N150,000, NRV N120,000. Line C: cost N90,000, NRV N100,000. Applying IAS 2 item by item, what is the total carrying amount of inventories?
questions.explanation: Taking the lower figure for each line gives N200,000 + N120,000 + N90,000 = N410,000. Option C is the total cost, which comes from comparing totals and lets the gain on A and C hide the loss on B. Option A is the total NRV, and option B wrongly takes the lowest possible combination by deducting B's shortfall twice.

questions.question: How does IAS 2 require write-downs of inventories to net realisable value normally to be made?

options.a: Only on items that have been physically damaged
options.b: Item by item, or by grouping similar or related items where appropriate
options.c: On the total of all inventories held by the entity
options.d: On the basis of a whole classification such as all finished goods

questions.explanation: Write-downs are usually made item by item, although similar or related items may sometimes be grouped. Option C is wrong because comparing totals allows profits on some items to cover losses on others. Option D is specifically considered inappropriate, and option A is too narrow since NRV can also fall because of lower selling prices or higher completion costs.

questions.question: Agege Bakery Ltd holds flour whose market price has fallen below its cost. The bread made from this flour is expected to sell at a price above its total cost. What should happen to the flour?

options.a: It is written down to its current market price
options.b: It is not written down below cost
options.d: It is written down to replacement cost

questions.explanation: Materials held for use in production are not written down below cost if the finished products they go into are expected to sell at or above cost. Options A and D would only be relevant if the bread itself were expected to sell below cost, in which case replacement cost may be the best measure of the flour's NRV. Option C has no basis since the flour is still usable.

questions.question: Under IAS 2, the cost of inventories comprises

options.a: Costs of conversion and all distribution costs
options.b: Costs of purchase, administrative overheads and storage costs
options.c: Costs of purchase and selling costs only
options.d: Costs of purchase, costs of conversion and other costs incurred in bringing the inventories to their present location and condition

questions.explanation: Cost of inventories is made up of costs of purchase, costs of conversion and other costs needed to bring the items to their present location and condition. Options C and A include selling and distribution costs, which are specifically excluded. Option B includes administrative overheads and general storage costs, which are also excluded unless they meet narrow conditions.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT included in the costs of purchase of inventories?

options.a: Import duties that cannot be recovered
options.b: Handling costs directly attributable to acquiring the goods
options.c: Transport costs to bring the goods to the warehouse
options.d: Value added tax that the entity can subsequently recover from the tax authorities

questions.explanation: Taxes that the entity can later recover are not a real cost to it, so they are excluded from cost of purchase. Options A, C and B are import duties and other non-recoverable taxes, transport and handling, which IAS 2 includes in costs of purchase.

questions.question: Which of the following costs may be included in the cost of inventories under IAS 2?

options.a: Administrative overheads that do not help bring inventories to their present location and condition
options.b: Fixed production overheads allocated on the basis of normal capacity

questions.explanation: Fixed production overheads are part of costs of conversion and are allocated to inventory based on the normal capacity of the production facilities. Options C, D and A are among the costs IAS 2 specifically excludes from cost and recognises as expenses when incurred.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the costs that IAS 2 excludes from the cost of inventories?

options.c: Direct labour used in making the goods
options.d: Storage costs not necessary in the production process

questions.explanation: Direct labour is a cost of conversion, so it is included in the cost of inventories. Options B, D and A are listed exclusions: abnormal waste, storage costs not needed before a further production stage, and selling costs are expensed when incurred.

questions.question: In which situation may storage costs be included in the cost of inventories?

options.a: When storage is necessary in the production process before a further production stage
options.b: When the storage costs relate to the head office records room
options.c: When the finished goods are stored awaiting sale to customers
options.d: When the entity chooses to capitalise them to increase profit

questions.explanation: Storage costs are excluded from cost unless they are necessary in the production process before a further stage, such as maturing a product before final processing. Option C is storage of finished goods awaiting sale, which is expensed. Option B is an administrative cost, and option D is not a valid reason under any standard.

questions.question: Apapa Imports Ltd bought goods with a list price of N1,000,000 and received a trade discount of N50,000. It also paid non-recoverable import duties of N80,000, recoverable VAT of N75,000, transport inward of N40,000, and N30,000 to advertise the goods. What is the cost of the inventories under IAS 2?
questions.explanation: Cost is N1,000,000 - N50,000 + N80,000 + N40,000 = N1,070,000, since trade discounts are deducted and only non-recoverable taxes and transport are added. Option A wrongly includes the recoverable VAT, and option D adds advertising, which is a selling cost. Option B ignores the trade discount.

questions.question: Ikorodu Furniture Ltd incurred the following in producing a batch of chairs: materials N800,000 (including N50,000 of abnormal waste), direct labour N300,000, production overheads N200,000 and general administration N100,000. What is the cost of the batch under IAS 2?
questions.explanation: Cost is materials excluding abnormal waste (N750,000) plus labour N300,000 plus production overheads N200,000, giving N1,250,000. Option A keeps the abnormal waste, option B adds the administration cost, and option D includes both items that IAS 2 excludes.

questions.question: Kano Oil Mills Ltd has fixed production overheads of N2,000,000 for the year. Normal capacity is 100,000 units, but only 80,000 units were produced because of low demand. Under IAS 2, how much of the fixed overhead is recognised as an expense in the period rather than included in inventory?
questions.explanation: Fixed overhead is absorbed at N2,000,000 / 100,000 = N20 per unit, so 80,000 units absorb N1,600,000 and the unallocated N400,000 is expensed. Option A spreads all the overhead over actual output, which IAS 2 does not allow when production is low. Option D expenses all of the fixed overhead, even though fixed production overheads are part of costs of conversion, and option B is the amount included in inventory, not the amount expensed.

questions.question: Lekki Jewellers Ltd makes unique custom pieces, each made for a named customer. Which cost formula must it use for these items?
questions.explanation: Items that are not ordinarily interchangeable, or goods produced and kept separate for specific projects, are costed by specific identification. Options D and B are used for large numbers of interchangeable items, and option C is not permitted under IAS 2 at all.

questions.question: An entity holds several groups of inventories. Which statement about its choice of cost formula is correct under IAS 2?

options.a: The same cost formula must be used for all inventories of a similar nature and use to the entity
options.b: Inventories in different branches must always use different formulas
options.c: A different cost formula may be chosen each year for the same inventories
options.d: FIFO must be used for all inventories without exception

questions.explanation: An entity must use the same cost formula for all inventories that have a similar nature and use, although different formulas may be justified for inventories of a different nature or use. Option C would destroy comparability, option D ignores weighted average and specific identification, and option B confuses location with nature and use.

questions.question: Ibadan Cement Distributors had opening inventory of 100 bags at N200 each. During the period it bought 300 bags at N220 each and then 200 bags at N250 each. It sold 450 bags. Using FIFO, what is the cost of closing inventory?
questions.explanation: Closing inventory is 600 - 450 = 150 bags, and under FIFO the bags left are the most recent purchases, so 150 x N250 = N37,500. Option D is the weighted average result, option C wrongly values the remaining bags at the opening price, and option A uses the middle purchase price.

questions.question: Ibadan Cement Distributors had opening inventory of 100 bags at N200 each. During the period it bought 300 bags at N220 each and then 200 bags at N250 each. It sold 450 bags. Using the weighted average cost formula (calculated on a periodic basis), what is the cost of closing inventory?
questions.explanation: Total cost is N20,000 + N66,000 + N50,000 = N136,000 for 600 bags, an average of about N226.67 per bag, so 150 bags cost N34,000. Option D is the FIFO result, option A uses a simple average of the three prices without weighting by quantity, and option B is the cost of sales, not closing inventory.

questions.question: Ibadan Cement Distributors had opening inventory of 100 bags at N200 each. During the period it bought 300 bags at N220 each and then 200 bags at N250 each. It sold 450 bags. Using FIFO, what is the cost of sales?
questions.explanation: Under FIFO the 450 bags sold are the 100 opening bags (N20,000), all 300 at N220 (N66,000) and 50 at N250 (N12,500), totalling N98,500. Option A is the weighted average cost of sales, and option B is the FIFO closing inventory. Option D wrongly charges the most recent purchases to cost of sales first.

questions.question: A large supermarket with many fast-moving items with similar margins wants to estimate the cost of its inventories. Which statement is correct under IAS 2?

options.a: It must use specific identification for every item
options.b: It must measure inventory at selling price
options.c: It may use LIFO because it is a retailer
options.d: It may use the retail method if the results approximate cost

questions.explanation: Techniques such as the standard cost method or the retail method may be used for convenience if the results approximate cost; the retail method is often used in retail for large numbers of fast-changing items with similar margins. Option A is impractical and only required for non-interchangeable items. Option B would overstate inventory, and option C is not permitted for anyone.

questions.question: Inventory written down to net realisable value last year is still held, and its net realisable value has now risen because selling prices have recovered. What does IAS 2 require?

options.a: Recognise the increase in other comprehensive income
options.b: Reverse the write-down so the new carrying amount is the lower of cost and the revised NRV
options.c: Increase the carrying amount to the new NRV even if it is above original cost
options.d: Leave the write-down in place because reversals are not permitted

questions.explanation: When the circumstances that caused the write-down no longer exist, the write-down is reversed, but only up to the original cost, so the item is carried at the lower of cost and the revised NRV. Option D is wrong because IAS 2 does require reversal. Option C would carry inventory above cost, and option A is wrong because the reversal reduces the inventory expense in profit or loss.

questions.question: Onitsha Spare Parts Ltd had an item costing N350,000 that was written down to its NRV of N300,000 last year. The item is still unsold, and its NRV is now N370,000. What amount of reversal is recognised this year?
questions.explanation: The write-down is reversed only up to original cost, so the carrying amount goes from N300,000 back to N350,000, a reversal of N50,000. Option B raises the item to N370,000, which is above cost. Option A is the excess of NRV over cost, and option C wrongly assumes reversals are not allowed.

questions.question: When inventories are sold, when is their carrying amount recognised as an expense under IAS 2?

options.a: In the period in which the related revenue is recognised
options.b: In the period in which the goods were purchased
options.c: At the end of the year in which the goods were produced
options.d: When cash is received from the customer

questions.explanation: The carrying amount of inventories sold is recognised as an expense in the same period as the related revenue, which matches cost of sales with sales. Option B would expense goods before they are sold, option D ties the expense to cash flow rather than the sale, and option C ignores whether the goods have actually been sold.

questions.question: How should a write-down of inventories to net realisable value, and a loss of inventories through theft, be treated under IAS 2?

options.a: Both are recognised as an expense in the period the write-down or loss occurs
options.b: Both are deferred and spread over future periods
options.c: Both are recognised in other comprehensive income
options.d: Both are adjusted against the opening retained earnings

questions.explanation: IAS 2 requires the amount of any write-down to NRV and all losses of inventories to be recognised as an expense in the period the write-down or loss occurs. Option B delays a loss that has already happened. Option C and option D bypass profit or loss, which IAS 2 does not allow for these items.

questions.question: Power Holding Nigeria Limited uses FIFO. Its opening inventory cost N4,000 and purchases for the year cost N15,450. Closing inventory has a cost of N3,500 and a net realisable value of N4,500. What is the cost of sales for the year?
questions.explanation: Cost of sales is opening inventory plus purchases less closing inventory: N4,000 + N15,450 - N3,500 = N15,950. Closing inventory stays at its cost of N3,500 because that is lower than its NRV of N4,500. N14,950 wrongly deducts the NRV of N4,500 instead of cost, and N19,450 forgets to deduct closing inventory at all.

questions.question: A farm in Epe harvests tomatoes from its plants. Which standard, rather than IAS 2, deals with the tomatoes at the point of harvest?
questions.explanation: Agricultural produce at the point of harvest, together with biological assets related to agricultural activity, is excluded from IAS 2 and dealt with by IAS 41 Agriculture. IFRS 9 is the other scope exclusion, but it covers financial instruments, not farm produce. IAS 16 deals with property, plant and equipment, and IAS 23 deals with borrowing costs.

questions.question: A manufacturing firm in Ikeja measures its finished goods using the standard cost method. How does IAS 2 treat this?

options.a: It is never allowed, as only FIFO is permitted
options.b: It is allowed if the results approximate cost
options.c: It is allowed only if the results equal selling price
options.d: It is allowed only for retailers, not manufacturers

questions.explanation: IAS 2 permits techniques such as the standard cost method and the retail method for convenience, provided the results approximate cost. The idea that only FIFO is permitted is wrong, because weighted average and specific identification are also allowed cost formulas. Limiting the method to retailers is also wrong; it is the retail method, not standard cost, that suits retailers.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: During the year ended 31 December 2015, a company changes its accounting policies. In line with IAS 8, how should the accountant treat the change (assuming it is not covered by specific transitional provisions)?

options.a: Recognise the full cumulative effect in current year profit or loss
options.b: Only disclose the change, without adjusting any figures
options.c: Apply the new policy retrospectively, adjusting the opening balance of equity for the earliest period presented and restating comparative figures
options.d: Apply the new policy prospectively from the date of change only, with no restatement

questions.explanation: A voluntary change in accounting policy is applied retrospectively under IAS 8, as if the new policy had always been used, so opening equity for the earliest period shown is adjusted and comparatives are restated. Option D is the treatment for a change in accounting estimate, not a policy. Option A would distort the current year, and option B leaves the figures uncomparable.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: According to IAS 8, how should a material error in the previous financial reporting period be accounted for in the current period?

options.a: By applying the correction prospectively from the current period
options.b: By retrospective restatement: restating the comparative amounts for the prior period in which the error occurred
options.c: By correcting it in current year profit or loss as an exceptional item
options.d: By disclosing it without changing any amounts

questions.explanation: IAS 8 requires material prior period errors to be corrected retrospectively, by restating the comparative figures for the period where the error happened (or the opening balances of the earliest period presented if it happened earlier). Option C would wrongly mix last year's mistake into this year's results. Option A is the treatment for changes in estimates, and option D leaves the error in the figures.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Which of the following is an objective of IAS 8?

options.a: To set the rules for depreciating property, plant and equipment
options.b: To prescribe the criteria for selecting and changing accounting policies, so as to enhance the relevance, reliability and comparability of financial statements
options.c: To prescribe how government grants should be recognised
options.d: To prescribe how borrowing costs are capitalised on qualifying assets

questions.explanation: IAS 8 aims to prescribe how accounting policies are selected and changed, and how changes in policies, estimates and errors are treated and disclosed, which makes financial statements more relevant, reliable and comparable. Option D belongs to IAS 23. Option C is IAS 20, and option A is IAS 16.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes accounting policies from accounting estimates under IAS 8?

options.a: Accounting policies are monetary amounts that involve judgement, while accounting estimates are the rules used to prepare financial statements
options.b: A change in accounting estimate is applied retrospectively, while a change in accounting policy is applied prospectively
options.c: Accounting policies and accounting estimates mean the same thing and are treated the same way
options.d: Accounting policies are the principles, bases, conventions, rules and practices applied in preparing financial statements, while accounting estimates are monetary amounts subject to measurement uncertainty, such as useful lives or allowances for doubtful debts

questions.explanation: Accounting policies are the specific principles, bases and rules an entity uses, while accounting estimates are the uncertain monetary amounts produced when applying those policies, such as a useful life, residual value or doubtful debt allowance. Option A swaps the two definitions. Option B reverses the treatments, since policy changes are retrospective and estimate changes are prospective. Option C is wrong because IAS 8 treats them differently.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: IAS 8 sets criteria that must be met before an entity changes an accounting policy. Under IAS 8, an entity shall change an accounting policy only if the change ______

options.a: is needed because the entity revised the useful life of an asset
options.b: increases reported profit for the year
options.c: is approved by the majority of shareholders at the AGM
options.d: is required by an IFRS, or results in financial statements providing reliable and more relevant information

questions.explanation: IAS 8 allows a change in accounting policy only when an IFRS requires it, or when the change gives reliable and more relevant information about transactions and events, for example adopting a new standard. Option B is not a valid reason, because policies cannot be changed just to improve results. Option C is not an IAS 8 criterion, and option A is a change in accounting estimate, not a policy change.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Accounting policies are ______

options.a: Broad basic assumptions which underlie the preparation of financial statements
options.b: Monetary amounts in the financial statements that are subject to measurement uncertainty
options.c: Financial accounting standards to be followed.
options.d: The specific principles, bases, conventions, rules and practices applied by an entity in preparing and presenting financial statements.

questions.explanation: Accounting policies are the specific principles, bases, conventions, rules and practices that an entity applies when preparing and presenting its financial statements, which is option D. Option B describes accounting estimates, such as useful lives or allowances for doubtful debts, which are the amounts produced when a policy is applied. Option A describes underlying assumptions such as going concern, and option C describes the standards themselves rather than the entity's own chosen policies.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT correct regarding the provisions of IAS 8 on accounting changes and error corrections?

options.a: A change in accounting estimate is reflected in the current and future periods.
options.b: A change in depreciation method (such as from an accelerated method to the straight-line method) is classified as a change in estimate.
options.c: A change in depreciation method (such as from accelerated method to the straight-line method) is classified as a change in accounting policy.
options.d: IAS 8 generally requires restating prior results to improve the comparability of financial statements.

questions.explanation: Under IAS 16 and IAS 8, a change in depreciation method (for example from an accelerated method to straight-line) reflects a change in the expected pattern of using up the asset, so it is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy - that makes option C the incorrect statement. Option B says the same thing correctly, and option A is also correct because estimate changes are applied prospectively to the current and future periods. Option D is correct too, since policy changes and prior period errors are generally applied retrospectively so that periods stay comparable.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Which term best describes applying a new accounting policy to transactions as if that policy had always been applied?
questions.explanation: Retrospective application means applying a new accounting policy to transactions, other events and conditions as if that policy had always been applied. Option B, retrospective restatement, is the term for correcting prior period errors as if they had never occurred. Option C, prospective application, applies the new policy only from the date of change, and option D is not a term used in IAS 8.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: All of the following should be treated as a change in accounting policy, except ______

options.a: A new accounting policy of capitalizing development cost as a project has become eligible for capitalization for the first time.
options.b: A new policy resulting from the requirement of a new IFRS.
options.c: To provide more relevant information, items of property, plant and equipment are now being measured at fair value, whereas they had previously been measured at cost.
options.d: All of these qualify as change in accounting policy.

questions.explanation: Applying a policy to transactions that differ in substance from earlier ones, or that occur for the first time, is not a change in accounting policy - so capitalising development costs once a project first becomes eligible is just applying the existing policy. Option B is a change in policy because a new IFRS requires it, and option C is a change in policy because moving from the cost model to the revaluation model changes the measurement basis. Option D is wrong because option A does not qualify.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: On March 25, 2018, the entity discovered that depreciation expense for 2017 was overstated. The 2017 financial statements were authorized for issue on April 1, 2018. What must the entity do?

options.a: Correct the 2017 financial statements before issuing them.
options.c: Restate the depreciation expense reported for 2017 in the comparative figures of the 2018 financial statements.

questions.explanation: The error was found on March 25, 2018, before the 2017 financial statements were authorised for issue on April 1, 2018, so the entity simply corrects the 2017 statements before issuing them. Option C would apply only if the statements had already been issued. Option B wrongly pushes the correction into 2018, and option D ignores a known error.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: On March 25, 2018, the entity discovered that depreciation expense for 2017 was overstated. The 2017 financial statements were authorized for issue on March 1, 2018. What must the entity do?

options.a: Reissue the 2017 financial statements with the correct depreciation expense.
options.c: Restate the depreciation expense reported for 2017 in the comparative figures of the 2018 financial statements.

questions.explanation: Here the 2017 financial statements were already authorised for issue on March 1, 2018 when the error was found, so IAS 8 requires retrospective restatement: the 2017 depreciation is corrected in the comparative figures presented in the 2018 financial statements. Option A is wrong because IAS 8 corrects errors through the comparatives, not by reissuing old statements. Option B treats the error like a change in estimate, and option D ignores it.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: How should a change in accounting estimate be accounted for?

options.a: As a non-adjusting event per IAS 10
options.b: Retrospectively with restated comparative financial statements
options.c: Retrospectively with an adjustment to opening retained earnings

questions.explanation: A change in accounting estimate, such as a revised useful life, is accounted for prospectively - it affects the current period and future periods only, and earlier figures are not restated. Options B and C describe retrospective treatment, which is used for changes in accounting policy and correction of errors. Option A is wrong because IAS 10 deals with events after the reporting period, not estimate changes.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: IAS 8 __________ disclosure of an impending change in accounting policy when an entity has yet to implement a new IFRS that has been issued but not yet come into effect.
questions.explanation: When a new IFRS has been issued but is not yet effective and the entity has not applied it, IAS 8 requires the entity to disclose that fact together with known or reasonably estimable information about the possible impact on its financial statements. Options C and D are too weak because the disclosure is compulsory, not just encouraged or allowed. Option A is the opposite of the rule.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Which, if any, of the following statements is correct? Statement 1 - An entity cannot change from applying straight line depreciation to reducing balance depreciation, or Statement 2 - A change in where depreciation is charged in the statement of profit or loss is a change in accounting estimate?
questions.explanation: Neither statement is correct. Statement 1 is false because an entity can change from straight-line to reducing balance depreciation when the pattern of using the asset changes - this is a change in accounting estimate. Statement 2 is false because changing where depreciation is presented in the statement of profit or loss is a change in presentation, which is a change in accounting policy, not an estimate. So options A, C and D are all wrong.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: It is __________ to make, or leave uncorrected, immaterial departures from IFRSs to achieve a particular presentation of an entity's financial position, financial performance or cash flows.
questions.explanation: IAS 8 states that it is inappropriate to make, or leave uncorrected, even immaterial departures from IFRSs in order to achieve a particular presentation, because deliberately using small departures to shape the picture defeats faithful presentation. Options A, C and D are wrong because such departures are never required, acceptable or advisable.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: A non-current asset was purchased for N200,000 at the start of year 1, when its expected economic life was ten years and its expected residual value was nil. The asset is depreciated by the straight-line method. A review at the start of year 2 (the current year) revealed that, due to technological change, the useful life of the asset is only six years in total. The revised estimate is applied from the beginning of year 2. What is the annual depreciation charge for year 2 and future years?
questions.explanation: A change in useful life is a change in estimate, so it is applied prospectively from the current year: the carrying amount at the start of year 2 is N200,000 - N20,000 = N180,000, and with five years left (years 2 to 6) the charge is N180,000 / 5 = N36,000 a year. Option A is the old charge of N200,000 / 10, which ignores the revision. Option B spreads the original cost over six years as if the new life had applied from the start, which is a retrospective approach, and option D divides N180,000 by four years, forgetting that year 2 itself still needs a charge.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: The main aim of IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Changes in Accounting Estimates and Errors is to:

options.a: Set out when revenue from contracts with customers should be recognised
options.b: Prescribe the minimum line items to be shown on the face of the statement of financial position
options.c: Enhance the comparability of an entity's financial statements with previous periods and with other entities
options.d: Prescribe how events after the reporting period should be adjusted for

questions.explanation: IAS 8 exists to improve comparability, both over time for the same entity and across different entities, by setting rules for policy changes, estimate changes and errors. Option B describes IAS 1, option A is the job of IFRS 15 and option D belongs to IAS 10.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: IAS 8 prescribes the treatment of three areas. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: Events after the reporting period are dealt with by IAS 10, not IAS 8. IAS 8 covers exactly three areas: changes in accounting policies (option C), changes in accounting estimates (option B) and errors (option D).

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Which of the following best describes how materiality is judged?

options.a: By the size or the nature of the item, or a combination of both, in the surrounding circumstances
options.b: By the size of the item alone, using a fixed percentage of profit before tax
options.c: By whether the item has been reviewed by the external auditor
options.d: By the nature of the item alone, regardless of its amount

questions.explanation: The test looks at the size and nature of an omission or misstatement in its surrounding circumstances, and either one, or both together, can be the deciding factor. Options B and D each look at only one factor, and option C has nothing to do with whether information would influence users.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Where an IFRS specifically applies to an item in the financial statements, the accounting policy for that item must be determined by:

options.a: The industry practice followed by the entity's main competitors
options.b: Management's own judgement of what gives the most relevant information
options.c: The policy that produces the highest reported profit for the year
options.d: Applying that Standard or Interpretation and any relevant implementation guidance

questions.explanation: When a Standard or Interpretation covers an item, the entity must follow it, together with any relevant implementation guidance. Management judgement (option B) is only used when no IFRS specifically applies, and options A and C are not bases for choosing a policy at all.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Kano Agro Ltd enters into a type of transaction for which no IFRS specifically applies. What must management do?

options.a: Apply the treatment required by the Nigerian tax authorities
options.b: Use its judgement to develop and apply a policy that gives relevant and reliable information
options.c: Choose any policy, as long as it is disclosed in the notes
options.d: Leave the transaction out of the financial statements until an IFRS is issued

questions.explanation: Where no IFRS specifically applies, management must use judgement to develop a policy whose result is information that is relevant to users' decisions and reliable. Leaving the item out (option D) would make the statements incomplete, and options A and C ignore the relevance and reliability test.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: When management develops a policy for an item not covered by any IFRS, the information must be reliable. Which of the following is NOT one of the features of reliable information listed in IAS 8?

options.a: It reflects the legal form of transactions rather than their economic substance
options.b: It is neutral, that is, free from bias
options.c: It is complete in all material respects
options.d: It represents faithfully the results and financial position of the entity

questions.explanation: Reliable information must reflect the economic substance of transactions and not merely their legal form, so option A reverses the actual requirement. Being neutral (option B), complete in every significant respect (option C) and faithfully representing results and position (option D) are all on the list.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: In the absence of an IFRS that specifically applies to a transaction, what should management refer to FIRST in making its judgement?

options.a: Accepted practices in the entity's industry
options.b: Requirements in IFRSs dealing with similar and related issues
options.c: The definitions and recognition criteria in the Conceptual Framework
options.d: The most recent pronouncements of other standard-setting bodies

questions.explanation: Management first looks at IFRSs that deal with similar and related issues, because they are the closest authoritative guidance. The Conceptual Framework (option C) is considered next, while pronouncements of other standard-setters and industry practice (options D and A) may be considered only so far as they do not conflict with these sources.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: An entity must apply consistent accounting policies for similar transactions in a period unless:

options.a: The items are below the entity's capitalisation threshold for the year
options.b: Management believes a different policy would give a higher profit for some items
options.c: An IFRS specifically requires or permits categorisation of items for which different policies may be appropriate
options.d: The transactions occurred in different months of the year

questions.explanation: Consistency is the rule for similar transactions, events and circumstances, with the only exception being where an IFRS itself requires or permits items to be grouped into categories with different policies. Options B, D and A are management preferences or timing points that do not justify inconsistent treatment.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Why are frequent changes in accounting policies considered undesirable?

options.a: They require the entity to change its auditors
options.b: They make it harder to compare an entity's financial statements with previous periods
options.c: They always reduce the entity's reported profit
options.d: They are prohibited by IAS 8 in all circumstances

questions.explanation: Users need to compare an entity's statements over time to spot trends, and frequent policy changes make comparisons with previous periods more difficult. Option D is wrong because changes are allowed when required by IFRS or when they give reliable and more relevant information, and options C and A are not consequences of a policy change.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: The directors of Ibadan Foods Plc want to change an accounting policy only because the new policy would increase this year's profit and help them meet a bonus target. No IFRS requires the change. Under IAS 8, this change is:

options.a: Permitted, as long as it is applied prospectively
options.b: Permitted, as long as the reason is disclosed
options.c: Not permitted, because it is neither required by IFRS nor shown to give reliable and more relevant information
options.d: Treated as a change in accounting estimate

questions.explanation: A voluntary policy change is allowed only when it makes the statements give reliable and more relevant information, and boosting profit for a bonus is not that. Applying it prospectively (option A) or disclosing the reason (option B) does not cure the lack of a valid ground, and option D is wrong because a choice of policy does not become an estimate just to avoid the rule.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: A new IFRS requires a change in accounting policy but contains no specific transitional provisions. How should the change be applied?

options.b: Only from the date the standard is first applied, with no adjustment to comparatives
options.c: As a correction of a prior period error

questions.explanation: Without specific transitional provisions, a change in accounting policy is applied retrospectively, as if the new policy had always been applied. Option D (prospective treatment) is the rule for changes in accounting estimates, option B would leave comparatives unadjusted, and option C is wrong because a policy change is not an error.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Abuja Logistics Ltd decides to classify certain delivery costs as cost of sales instead of administrative expenses. This is a change in accounting policy relating to:
questions.explanation: Changing where costs are classified, such as cost of sales versus administrative expenses, is a change in presentation, and any change in recognition, measurement or presentation is a change in accounting policy. Recognition (option C) is about whether an item is capitalised or written off, measurement (option B) is about cost or valuation, and option A is wrong because this is a policy change, not an estimate.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: A company that has always written off a certain type of expenditure as an expense decides to capitalise it instead. This change concerns which aspect of accounting policy?
questions.explanation: Deciding whether expenditure is capitalised or written off is a recognition question, so a change here is a change in accounting policy. Measurement (option D) is about the basis used, such as cost or valuation, presentation (option B) is about classification, and option A is the test of whether an item matters to users, not one of the three aspects.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Lekki Properties Ltd has measured its investment properties using the cost model. It switches to the fair value model because it believes this gives reliable and more relevant information. This is:

options.a: A change in accounting policy affecting presentation
options.b: A change in accounting estimate applied prospectively
options.c: A change in accounting policy affecting measurement
options.d: The correction of a prior period error

questions.explanation: Moving from the cost model to the fair value model changes the measurement basis, which makes it a change in accounting policy affecting measurement. Option B is wrong because a change in measurement basis is never an estimate change, option A is wrong because nothing is reclassified, and option D is wrong because the old treatment was not a mistake.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Enugu Steel Ltd has never held investment property before. This year it buys its first investment property and adopts the fair value model for it. Under IAS 8, adopting this policy is:

options.a: A change in accounting policy that requires a third statement of financial position
options.b: A change in accounting policy that must be applied retrospectively
options.c: A change in accounting estimate that must be applied prospectively
options.d: Not a change in accounting policy, since it applies a policy to a type of transaction that did not occur previously

questions.explanation: Applying a policy to transactions that did not occur before, or that differ in substance from earlier ones, is not a change in accounting policy; it is simply choosing a suitable policy for a new type of transaction. That is why options B and A, which treat it as a policy change, are wrong, and option C is wrong because no estimate has been revised.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: The initial application of a policy to revalue property, plant and equipment under IAS 16 is:

options.a: A change in accounting estimate accounted for prospectively under IAS 8
options.b: A change in accounting policy accounted for retrospectively under IAS 8
options.c: Not a change in accounting policy, since revaluation is a new type of transaction
options.d: A change in accounting policy, but accounted for under IAS 16 rather than IAS 8

questions.explanation: Starting to revalue assets under IAS 16 or IAS 38 is a change in accounting policy, but the standards themselves give the treatment, so it is dealt with as a revaluation under those standards rather than by IAS 8's retrospective rule. Option B applies the wrong standard, option A wrongly calls it an estimate, and option C wrongly says it is not a policy change.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: When a change in accounting policy is applied retrospectively, the entity should adjust:

options.a: The opening balance of each affected component of equity for the earliest prior period presented, and the other comparative amounts
options.b: Only the notes, leaving all amounts in the primary statements unchanged
options.c: Only the profit or loss of the current period, with no change to comparatives
options.d: The closing balance of retained earnings for the current period only

questions.explanation: Retrospective application adjusts the opening balance of each affected item of equity for the earliest prior period presented, plus the other comparative amounts, as if the new policy had always applied. Option C describes prospective treatment, and options D and B would leave the comparative figures inconsistent with the new policy.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Jos Textiles Plc presents comparatives for one previous year. In its financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2025 it applies a change in accounting policy retrospectively. Which statements of financial position must it present?

options.a: As at 31 December 2025 and 31 December 2024 only
options.b: As at 31 December 2025, 31 December 2024 and 1 January 2024
options.c: As at 31 December 2025, 31 December 2024 and 1 January 2025
options.d: As at 31 December 2025 and 1 January 2025 only

questions.explanation: IAS 1 requires an extra statement of financial position at the beginning of the earliest comparative period when a policy is applied retrospectively; with 2024 as the comparative year, that date is 1 January 2024. Option A is what would be shown with no policy change, and options C and D use the start of the current year instead of the start of the earliest comparative period.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Under IAS 8, applying a requirement is impracticable when:

options.a: Applying it would take longer than one month to complete
options.b: Applying it would reduce the entity's reported profit
options.c: Management would prefer not to restate the comparative figures
options.d: The entity cannot apply it after making every reasonable effort to do so

questions.explanation: Impracticable has a strict meaning: the entity has made every reasonable effort and still cannot apply the requirement. A lower profit (option B), extra time (option A) or management's preference (option C) do not make a requirement impracticable.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the situations in which IAS 8 regards retrospective application or restatement for a prior period as impracticable?

options.a: It requires assumptions about what management's intent would have been in that period
options.b: The effects of the retrospective application are not determinable
options.c: It requires significant estimates that cannot be objectively separated from information that came later
options.d: The restatement would significantly reduce retained earnings

questions.explanation: A large reduction in retained earnings is simply the effect of the restatement, not a reason it cannot be done. The three recognised situations are effects that cannot be determined (option B), the need for assumptions about management's past intent (option A) and significant estimates that cannot be objectively separated from hindsight information (option C).

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: If retrospective application of a change in accounting policy to all prior periods is impracticable, the entity should:

options.a: Abandon the change in policy and continue with the old policy
options.b: Apply the new policy retrospectively from the earliest date that is practicable
options.c: Apply the new policy only to transactions arising after the end of the current period
options.d: Treat the change as a change in accounting estimate

questions.explanation: Impracticability does not cancel the change; the entity applies the new policy retrospectively from the earliest date that is practicable. Option A wrongly drops the change, option D wrongly reclassifies it as an estimate, and option C goes much further than necessary by ignoring periods where restatement is possible.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Which disclosure is required for a VOLUNTARY change in accounting policy but not for a change required by an IFRS?

options.a: The adjustment relating to periods before those presented, to the extent practicable
options.b: The nature of the change in accounting policy
options.c: The reason why the new accounting policy provides reliable and more relevant information
options.d: The amount of the adjustment to each affected item for the current and previous periods

questions.explanation: A voluntary change is justified only because it gives reliable and more relevant information, so the entity must explain that reason. The nature of the change (option B) and the amounts of the adjustments (options D and A) must be disclosed for both kinds of change.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Which disclosure is required for a change in accounting policy made because of an IFRS, but not for a voluntary change?

options.a: A description of any transitional provisions
options.b: The nature of the change in accounting policy
options.c: An explanation if retrospective application is impracticable
options.d: The reason why the new policy provides reliable and more relevant information

questions.explanation: Transitional provisions come from the new standard, so describing them applies only when the change is required by an IFRS, along with the title of that standard. The nature of the change (option B) and the impracticability explanation (option C) apply to both kinds of change, while the reason for more relevant information (option D) applies only to voluntary changes.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: An accounting estimate is needed for an item in the financial statements when:

options.a: The item was recorded incorrectly in a prior period
options.b: No IFRS specifically applies to the item
options.c: The entity changes the measurement basis of the item
options.d: The item cannot be measured with precision and there is some uncertainty about it

questions.explanation: Estimates are needed where an amount cannot be measured precisely and is uncertain, so it depends partly on management's judgement. Option B is the situation where management develops a policy, option A describes a prior period error, and option C is a change in accounting policy.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of an item that requires an accounting estimate?

options.b: The decision to measure investment property at fair value rather than cost
options.c: The useful lives of non-current assets
options.d: The fair value of financial assets or liabilities

questions.explanation: Choosing fair value instead of cost is a choice of measurement basis, which is an accounting policy, not an estimate. Inventory obsolescence (option A), useful lives (option C) and the fair value of financial assets or liabilities (option D) are all given as items needing management estimates.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Owerri Bottling Ltd changes the depreciation method for its delivery vans from straight line to reducing balance because the vans' benefits are now used up mainly in their early years. How is this accounted for?

options.a: As a change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively
options.b: As a change in accounting policy, applied prospectively
options.c: As a change in accounting policy, applied retrospectively
options.d: As a correction of a prior period error, by retrospective restatement

questions.explanation: The depreciation method reflects the pattern in which an asset's benefits are used up, so choosing between straight line and reducing balance is an accounting estimate, and a change is applied prospectively. Options C and B wrongly treat it as a policy change, and option D is wrong because the old method was a reasonable estimate, not a mistake.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: When it is difficult to tell whether a change is a change in accounting policy or a change in accounting estimate, IAS 8 requires the change to be treated as:

options.a: A matter for the auditor to decide

questions.explanation: Where the two cannot be clearly distinguished, the change is treated as a change in accounting estimate, so it is applied prospectively. Option B reverses the rule, option C is wrong because nothing was done incorrectly, and option A is not how IAS 8 settles the matter.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: A change in the measurement basis applied to an item, such as moving from the cost model to the revaluation model, is:

options.d: Neither a change in policy nor a change in estimate

questions.explanation: Measurement is one of the three aspects of accounting policy, so changing the measurement basis is a change in accounting policy and not a change in estimate. Option C confuses the basis with the amounts estimated under it, option A wrongly implies the old basis was a mistake, and option D ignores the clear rule.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Changes in accounting estimates are not corrections of errors because they:

options.a: Always relate to periods before those presented
options.b: Result from new information or new developments
options.c: Arise from mathematical mistakes in earlier calculations
options.d: Are required by a new or revised IFRS

questions.explanation: A change in estimate reflects a fresh assessment of the present status and expected future benefits or obligations of assets and liabilities, based on new information or developments, so the earlier figure was not wrong. Option D describes a policy change required by a standard, and options A and C point to situations that suggest a prior period error.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Prospective application of a change in accounting estimate means that the effect of the change is recognised:

options.a: As an adjustment to opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented
options.b: By restating the comparative figures for all prior periods presented
options.c: In the current period and the future periods affected by the change
options.d: Only in the notes, with no effect on profit or loss

questions.explanation: Prospective treatment leaves past figures alone and puts the effect into the period of change and any future periods affected. Options B and A describe retrospective treatment, which is used for policy changes and errors, and option D is wrong because the effect does go through profit or loss.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Kaduna Motors Ltd revises an estimate that affects only the current year, with no effect on later years. Where is the effect of the change recognised?

options.a: In profit or loss for the current period and all future periods
options.b: In profit or loss for the current period only
options.c: By restating the prior year comparative figures
options.d: As an adjustment to opening retained earnings

questions.explanation: When a change in estimate affects only the period in which it is made, its effect goes into profit or loss for that period. Option A applies only when the change also affects future periods, and options D and C are retrospective treatments that are never used for estimate changes.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: For a change in accounting estimate, which of the following must be disclosed?

options.a: The title of the Standard that required the change
options.b: The reason why the new estimate gives reliable and more relevant information
options.c: The nature and amount of the change that affects the current period or is expected to affect future periods
options.d: Restated comparative figures for every prior period presented

questions.explanation: IAS 8 requires the nature and amount of a change in estimate that affects the current period or future periods, and if the future effect cannot practicably be estimated, that fact must be stated. Options B and A are disclosures for changes in accounting policy, and option D is wrong because estimate changes are not applied retrospectively.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Omissions from, and misstatements in, an entity's financial statements for one or more prior periods, arising from failure to use, or misuse of, reliable information that was available when those statements were authorised for issue, are called:
questions.explanation: This is the definition of prior period errors: the correct information existed and could reasonably have been obtained and used at the time, but was not used or was misused. Changes in estimates (option A) come from new information, policy changes (option B) are deliberate choices of a different policy, and non-adjusting events (option D) belong to IAS 10.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: While preparing its 2025 financial statements, Aba Leather Ltd discovers that its 2024 depreciation charge was understated because a clerk entered the wrong figure in the calculation. The information needed was available when the 2024 statements were approved. This is:

options.d: A transaction that did not occur previously

questions.explanation: A mathematical or clerical mistake using information that was available at the time is a prior period error and is corrected retrospectively. It is not a change in estimate (option C) because no new information has emerged, not a policy change (option A) because the policy is unchanged, and option D has nothing to do with this situation.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Ilorin Cement Plc had estimated a kiln's useful life at 15 years. This year, new information about wear shows that its total useful life will be only 10 years. The revision is:

options.a: A change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively
options.b: A prior period error, corrected by retrospective restatement
options.c: A change in accounting policy, applied retrospectively
options.d: A change in measurement basis, applied retrospectively

questions.explanation: Useful life is an estimate, and revising it because of new information is a change in accounting estimate, recognised in the current and future periods. Option B is wrong because the original estimate was reasonable when made, and options C and D are wrong because the measurement basis and policy have not changed.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: To the extent that a change in accounting estimate gives rise to changes in assets and liabilities, it is recognised by:

options.a: Creating a separate reserve within equity for the change
options.b: Disclosing the change only, without changing carrying amounts
options.c: Adjusting the carrying amount of the asset or liability at the start of the earliest period presented
options.d: Adjusting the carrying amount of the affected asset or liability in the period of change

questions.explanation: Where an estimate change affects assets or liabilities, their carrying amounts are adjusted in the period in which the change is made. Option C is a retrospective approach, option B would leave the carrying amount out of date, and option A is not a treatment IAS 8 uses.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Ogun Packaging Ltd bought a machine for N12,000,000. It was depreciated straight line over 8 years with nil residual value. At the start of Year 4 (after 3 full years of use), management revises the remaining useful life to 3 years. What is the depreciation charge for Year 4?
questions.explanation: The carrying amount at the start of Year 4 is N12,000,000 - (3 x N1,500,000) = N7,500,000, and this is spread over the revised remaining life: N7,500,000 / 3 = N2,500,000. Option C is the old charge, option D wrongly spreads the original cost over the new total life of 6 years, and option B divides cost rather than carrying amount by the remaining life.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Using the same facts (cost N12,000,000, 8-year straight line life, nil residual value, remaining life revised to 3 years at the start of Year 4 after 3 years of use), what is the machine's carrying amount at the end of Year 4?
questions.explanation: At the start of Year 4 the carrying amount is N7,500,000, and the revised Year 4 charge is N7,500,000 / 3 = N2,500,000, leaving N5,000,000. Option D uses the old charge of N1,500,000 for Year 4, option A recalculates all four years at N2,000,000 as if the change were retrospective, and option B forgets to charge Year 4 depreciation.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Calabar Marine Ltd bought a boat for N30,000,000, with a 10-year useful life and a residual value of N2,000,000, depreciated straight line. At the start of Year 5 (after 4 years), the residual value estimate is revised to N5,600,000; the total useful life is unchanged. What is the depreciation charge for Year 5?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation was (N30,000,000 - N2,000,000) / 10 = N2,800,000, so the carrying amount after 4 years is N18,800,000. Applying the change prospectively, (N18,800,000 - N5,600,000) / 6 remaining years = N2,200,000. Option B is the old charge, option A wrongly restarts from cost over 10 years, and option C ignores the residual value.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Warri Energy Ltd bought a generator for N48,000,000 at the start of Year 1, to be depreciated straight line over 12 years with nil residual value. At the start of Year 3, after two full years of use, a review shows that the generator's total useful life will be only 7 years. What is the depreciation charge for Year 3?
questions.explanation: The carrying amount at the start of Year 3 is N48,000,000 - (2 x N4,000,000) = N40,000,000, and the remaining life is 7 - 2 = 5 years, giving N40,000,000 / 5 = N8,000,000. Option B is the old charge, option A divides the original cost by the new total life, and option C uses only 4 remaining years instead of 5.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: For Warri Energy Ltd (generator cost N48,000,000, originally depreciated at N4,000,000 a year; revised charge of N8,000,000 a year from Year 3 after its total life was cut to 7 years), by how much is Year 3 profit lower than it would have been under the old estimate?

options.c: Nil, because the change is taken to retained earnings

questions.explanation: Under prospective application, Year 3 bears the new charge of N8,000,000 instead of N4,000,000, so profit is N4,000,000 lower, and Years 1 and 2 are not reopened. Option D counts the whole new charge rather than the increase, option B adds a catch-up for earlier years as if the change were retrospective, and option C is wrong because estimate changes go through profit or loss, not retained earnings.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Akure Farms Ltd bought a tractor for N18,000,000, depreciated straight line over 6 years with nil residual value. At the start of Year 3, after 2 years of use, new information shows that the tractor's total useful life will be 8 years. What is the depreciation charge for Year 3?
questions.explanation: The carrying amount at the start of Year 3 is N18,000,000 - (2 x N3,000,000) = N12,000,000, spread over the remaining 8 - 2 = 6 years, giving N2,000,000. Option D keeps the old charge, option A spreads the original cost over the new total life, and option B divides the carrying amount by the total life instead of the remaining life.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Sokoto Haulage Ltd bought a truck for N32,000,000, depreciated straight line over 8 years with nil residual value. At the start of Year 3 it changes to the reducing balance method at 25% a year because this better reflects how the truck's benefits are used up. What is the depreciation charge for Year 3?
questions.explanation: A change in depreciation method is a change in estimate, so 25% is applied to the carrying amount at the start of Year 3: N32,000,000 - (2 x N4,000,000) = N24,000,000, and 25% of that is N6,000,000. Option B is the old straight line charge, option C applies 25% to cost, and option A recalculates as if reducing balance had always been used, which is a retrospective approach.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: In 2025, Onitsha Traders Ltd discovers that closing inventory at 31 December 2024 was overstated by N3,000,000 through a counting mistake. Profit for 2024 was originally reported as N20,000,000. Ignoring tax, what is the restated profit for 2024 shown in the comparative figures?
questions.explanation: Overstated closing inventory makes cost of sales too low and profit too high, so the 2024 profit is restated to N20,000,000 - N3,000,000 = N17,000,000. Option D adds the error instead of removing it, option C leaves the comparative uncorrected as if the error were dealt with in 2025, and option A deducts the error twice.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Yola Hotels Ltd reported retained earnings of N50,000,000 at 31 December 2024. In 2025 it discovers that N4,000,000 of repair costs incurred in 2024 were wrongly capitalised as property, plant and equipment. Ignoring tax and depreciation, what is the restated retained earnings at 1 January 2025?
questions.explanation: Repair costs should have been expensed in 2024, so 2024 profit and therefore retained earnings were overstated by N4,000,000; the restated figure is N50,000,000 - N4,000,000 = N46,000,000. Option B adds the amount, option D leaves retained earnings unchanged as if the error went through 2025 profit or loss, and option C deducts it twice.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Ikeja Estates Ltd bought an investment property for N80,000,000 on 1 January 2023 and used the cost model, depreciating it by N2,000,000 a year. In 2025 it changes to the fair value model (a voluntary change applied retrospectively), presenting 2024 comparatives. Fair values were N90,000,000 at 31 December 2023 and N95,000,000 at 31 December 2024. Ignoring tax, what is the adjustment to retained earnings at 1 January 2024?
questions.explanation: Under the cost model the carrying amount at 31 December 2023 was N80,000,000 - N2,000,000 = N78,000,000; under the fair value model it would have been N90,000,000, so opening retained earnings at 1 January 2024 rise by N12,000,000. Option A forgets to add back the 2023 depreciation, while options B and D use the 31 December 2024 fair value, which belongs to the comparative year itself rather than the opening balance.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Using the same facts for Ikeja Estates Ltd (cost model depreciation N2,000,000 a year; fair values N90,000,000 at 31 December 2023 and N95,000,000 at 31 December 2024; change to fair value model applied retrospectively), by how much does the restated 2024 profit differ from the profit originally reported for 2024?
questions.explanation: Under the fair value model 2024 profit includes a fair value gain of N95,000,000 - N90,000,000 = N5,000,000 and no depreciation, so compared with the old N2,000,000 depreciation charge profit rises by N7,000,000. Option D forgets that the depreciation charge disappears, option A deducts depreciation instead of reversing it, and option B lumps the earlier years' effect into 2024 instead of opening retained earnings.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Benin Pharma Ltd changes its inventory cost formula from FIFO to weighted average in 2025 and applies the change retrospectively with 2024 comparatives. Inventory was: 31 December 2023 - FIFO N18,000,000, weighted average N16,500,000; 31 December 2024 - FIFO N25,000,000, weighted average N22,000,000. Profit for 2024 under FIFO was N40,000,000. Ignoring tax, what is the restated 2024 profit?
questions.explanation: Lower closing inventory at 31 December 2024 (N3,000,000 less) raises cost of sales and cuts profit, while lower opening inventory at 1 January 2024 (N1,500,000 less) reduces cost of sales and adds to profit: N40,000,000 - N3,000,000 + N1,500,000 = N38,500,000. Option C ignores the opening inventory effect, option D reverses the direction of the adjustments, and option A deducts both differences.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: For Benin Pharma Ltd (inventory at 31 December 2023 - FIFO N18,000,000, weighted average N16,500,000; at 31 December 2024 - FIFO N25,000,000, weighted average N22,000,000; change to weighted average applied retrospectively with 2024 comparatives), what is the adjustment to retained earnings at 1 January 2024? Ignore tax.
questions.explanation: Opening retained earnings at 1 January 2024 reflect inventory at 31 December 2023, which falls by N18,000,000 - N16,500,000 = N1,500,000 under the new formula, so retained earnings decrease by N1,500,000. Option B uses the 2024 difference, which belongs in the comparative year's profit, option D adds both years, and option C has the wrong direction.

questions.topic: IAS 8 Accounting Policies, Estimates and Errors
questions.question: Minna Mills Ltd discovers in 2025 that depreciation of N1,500,000 on a machine was omitted from its 2024 financial statements by oversight; the amount is material. Profit for 2024 was originally reported as N26,000,000. Ignoring tax, how should the omission be dealt with in the 2025 financial statements?

options.a: Restate 2024 profit to N24,500,000; also charge N1,500,000 in 2025 profit or loss
options.b: Keep 2024 profit at N26,000,000; charge N1,500,000 in 2025 profit or loss
options.c: Restate 2024 profit to N27,500,000; no charge in 2025 profit or loss
options.d: Restate 2024 profit to N24,500,000; no charge in 2025 profit or loss

questions.explanation: An oversight using information available at the time is a prior period error, so the 2024 comparative is restated to N26,000,000 - N1,500,000 = N24,500,000 and the correction does not pass through 2025 profit or loss. Option B wrongly treats the error in the current year, option C adds the omitted charge instead of deducting it, and option A counts the expense twice by also charging it in 2025.

questions.question: Ezechukwu Nigeria Limited bought an asset for N2,500,000 in January 2023. The company depreciates assets on the reducing balance method. The estimated residual (scrap) value of the asset is N420,175 and the expected useful life is 5 years. Using R = (1 - n-th root of (S/C)) x 100, what is the depreciation rate and the depreciation charge for year 1?
questions.explanation: S/C = 420,175 / 2,500,000 = 0.16807, and the fifth root of 0.16807 is 0.7, so R = (1 - 0.7) x 100 = 30%. Year 1 depreciation is 30% x N2,500,000 = N750,000. Option C applies the 30% rate to cost less scrap value (N2,079,825), but reducing balance applies the rate to the full opening carrying amount, with no deduction for scrap value. Option A is a straight-line rate (100%/5), and option B confuses the S/C ratio with the rate.

questions.question: Ezechukwu Nigeria Limited bought an asset for N2,500,000 in January 2023 and depreciates it on the reducing balance method at 30% per annum (residual value N420,175, useful life 5 years). What is the carrying amount of the asset at the end of year 3?
questions.explanation: Each year the 30% rate is applied to the opening carrying amount: year 1 depreciation N750,000 leaves N1,750,000, year 2 N525,000 leaves N1,225,000, and year 3 N367,500 leaves N857,500 (accumulated depreciation N1,642,500). Option D is the carrying amount after only two years. Option B wrongly charges 30% of the original cost every year, and option A is the carrying amount after four years.

questions.question: Jugunnu bought a motor vehicle for N1,150,000 in January 2022. She depreciated it at 20% per annum on a straight line basis on its depreciable amount (cost less estimated scrap value of N150,000).
