The vehicle was disposed of in December 2024 for N720,000 after incurring N25,000 to put it in good sellable condition. What was the profit or loss on disposal?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation is 20% x (N1,150,000 - N150,000) = N200,000, so after three years (2022 to 2024) accumulated depreciation is N600,000 and the carrying amount is N550,000. Net disposal proceeds are N720,000 - N25,000 = N695,000, giving a profit of N695,000 - N550,000 = N145,000. Option B forgets to deduct the N25,000 cost of getting it ready for sale. Options C and A charge only two years of depreciation.

questions.question: From the information provided, determine the cost to be capitalised in the statement of financial position. Motor car N4,500,000; Registration number N150,000; Road license fees N25,000; Delivery charge for the car N35,000; Cost of testing the car N100,000; Purchase of office premises N8,000,000; Legal fees associated with purchase of office N800,000; Driver's wages for first year of operation N1,200,000. What is the cost of the motor vehicle to be capitalised?
questions.explanation: Under IAS 16 the cost includes the purchase price plus costs directly needed to get the asset ready for use: N4,500,000 + N150,000 registration + N35,000 delivery + N100,000 testing = N4,785,000. Option B adds the N25,000 road licence, which is a recurring running cost and is expensed. Option C leaves out the testing cost, which IAS 16 specifically allows, and option D adds the driver's wages, which are an operating expense.

questions.question: From the information provided, determine the cost to be capitalised in the statement of financial position. Motor car N4,500,000; Registration number N150,000; Road license fees N25,000; Delivery charge for the car N35,000; Cost of testing the car N100,000; Purchase of office premises N8,000,000; Legal fees associated with purchase of office N800,000; Driver's wages for first year of operation N1,200,000. What is the cost of the office premises (land and building) to be capitalised?
questions.explanation: Legal fees on buying property are directly attributable costs of acquiring it, so the capitalised cost is N8,000,000 + N800,000 = N8,800,000. Option A leaves out the legal fees and option C wrongly deducts them. Option D adds the driver's wages of N1,200,000, which relate to running the business, not to the building.

questions.question: An asset (Motor Car) was bought for N2,500,000 with an expected residual value of N250,000. If the useful life of the asset is 5 years, determine the annual depreciation using the straight-line method of depreciation
questions.explanation: Straight-line depreciation is (cost - residual value) / useful life = (N2,500,000 - N250,000) / 5 = N2,250,000 / 5 = N450,000 a year. Option B forgets to deduct the residual value, and option C adds the residual value instead of subtracting it. Option D divides by 10 instead of the 5-year useful life.

questions.question: ABC bought a motor vehicle for N500,000 with an expected useful life of 5 years. The expected residual value of the asset is N163,840. The reducing balance method of depreciation is used. What is the annual depreciation rate?
questions.explanation: The reducing balance rate is r = 1 - (residual / cost)^(1/n) = 1 - (163,840 / 500,000)^(1/5) = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2, or 20%. Option B is what you get by treating it like straight-line ((500,000 - 163,840) / 5 as a percentage of cost). Option C is just the ratio 163,840 / 500,000, and option D is the fraction of the balance kept each year (0.8), not the rate charged.

questions.question: ABC bought a motor vehicle for N500,000 with an expected useful life of 5 years. The expected residual value of the asset is N163,840. The reducing balance method of depreciation is used. What is the depreciation charge for year 3?
questions.explanation: At a 20% rate the carrying amount falls from N500,000 to N400,000 in year 1 and N320,000 in year 2, so the year 3 charge is 20% x N320,000 = N64,000. Option B is the straight-line charge (N500,000 - N163,840) / 5. Option C is the year 2 charge, and option D wrongly applies 20% to the original cost every year.

questions.question: The objective of IAS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment is to prescribe the accounting treatment for PPE so that users of financial statements can

options.a: determine the market value of the entity's shares at the reporting date
options.b: discern information about an entity's investment in its PPE and the changes in that investment
options.c: compare the selling prices of the entity's inventories with their cost
options.d: assess the entity's ability to settle its short-term liabilities as they fall due

questions.explanation: IAS 16 exists so that users can see how much an entity has invested in its property, plant and equipment and how that investment changes over time. Option A is about share valuation and option D describes liquidity analysis, neither of which is the aim of IAS 16. Option C relates to inventory measurement, which is dealt with under IAS 2.

questions.question: Tangible items that are held for use in the production or supply of goods or services, for rentals to others, or for administrative purposes, and are expected to be used during more than one period, are called
questions.explanation: This is the IAS 16 definition of property, plant and equipment: tangible, held for use (not for sale), and used for more than one period. Option B is wrong because inventories are held for sale or consumed in production, and option C is wrong because intangible assets have no physical substance. Option D is wrong because PPE is used over more than one period, so it is non-current.

questions.question: Ikeja Motors Ltd sells new cars. Which of the following items would it classify as property, plant and equipment?

options.a: Cash held in the company's bank account
options.b: The showroom building from which it sells the cars
options.c: The new cars displayed in the showroom for sale to customers
options.d: Amounts owed by customers who bought cars on credit

questions.explanation: The showroom is a tangible item held for use in supplying goods and will be used for more than one period, so it is PPE. Option C is wrong because cars held for sale are the dealer's inventory. Options A and D are financial assets (cash and receivables), not tangible items held for use.

questions.question: The amount of cash or cash equivalents paid, or the fair value of the other consideration given, to acquire an asset at the time of its acquisition or construction is the asset's
questions.explanation: Cost is what is given up to acquire or construct the asset, measured at the time of acquisition or construction. Option D is cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment, option C is the estimated disposal amount at the end of useful life, and option B is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use.

questions.question: The cost of an asset, or other amount substituted for cost, less its residual value is known as the
questions.explanation: Depreciable amount is the part of the cost that will be spread over the useful life, so it is cost less residual (scrap) value. Option A deducts accumulated depreciation and impairment, not residual value. Option C is the total depreciation charged to date, and option D is used for impairment testing.

questions.question: The systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an asset over its estimated useful life is called
questions.explanation: Depreciation is the systematic spreading of the depreciable amount over the useful life. Option C is a reduction of carrying amount to recoverable amount, not a systematic allocation. Option B restates an asset to fair value, and option A relates to grants under IAS 20, not to the cost of PPE.

questions.question: The carrying amount of an item of property, plant and equipment is the amount at which it is recognised after deducting

options.a: the costs of disposal from its fair value
options.b: import duties and non-refundable purchase taxes
options.d: any accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment losses

questions.explanation: Carrying amount is cost (or revalued amount) minus accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment losses. Option C gives the depreciable amount, not the carrying amount. Option A describes fair value less costs of disposal, and option B lists items that are added to cost, not deducted.

questions.question: The price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date is
questions.explanation: This is the definition of fair value, an exit price between market participants (see IFRS 13). Option C is the present value of cash flows from using the asset, option D is what was paid to acquire it, and option A is the estimated disposal amount at the end of useful life.

questions.question: An impairment loss is the amount by which

options.a: the recoverable amount of an asset exceeds its carrying amount
options.b: the carrying amount of an asset exceeds its recoverable amount
options.c: the cost of an asset exceeds its residual value
options.d: the fair value of an asset exceeds its cost

questions.explanation: An impairment loss arises when an asset is carried at more than it can recover, so it is carrying amount minus recoverable amount. Option A is the reverse situation, where there is no impairment. Option C is the depreciable amount, and option D would be a revaluation increase, not a loss.

questions.question: Recoverable amount is the

options.a: lower of an asset's fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use
options.b: lower of an asset's carrying amount and its residual value
options.c: higher of an asset's cost and its fair value
options.d: higher of an asset's fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use

questions.explanation: Recoverable amount is the HIGHER of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, because a sensible entity would either sell or keep using the asset, whichever gives more. Option A wrongly uses the lower figure. Options C and B mix up cost, carrying amount and residual value, which are not part of this definition.

questions.question: The estimated amount that an entity would currently obtain from disposal of an asset, after deducting the estimated costs of disposal, if the asset were already of the age and in the condition expected at the end of its useful life, is the
questions.explanation: This is residual (scrap) value: today's estimate of what the asset would fetch, net of disposal costs, if it were already at the end of its useful life. Option C is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, option D is a current exit price for the asset in its present condition, and option A is cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment.

questions.question: Under IAS 16, the useful life of an asset may be expressed as either the period over which it is expected to be available for use, or

options.a: the period until its fair value falls to zero
options.b: the number of years its manufacturer's warranty lasts
options.c: the period remaining until its loan is fully repaid
options.d: the number of production or similar units expected to be obtained from it

questions.explanation: Useful life can be measured in time or in output: the number of production or similar units the entity expects to get from the asset. Options C and B tie useful life to financing or warranty terms, which do not define how long the entity will use the asset. Option A is wrong because useful life is about expected use by the entity, not market value.

questions.question: Under IAS 16, the cost of an item of property, plant and equipment is recognised as an asset if, and only if,

options.a: the item has been fully paid for in cash and it will be used for more than one period
options.b: it is probable that future economic benefits associated with the item will flow to the entity and its cost can be measured reliably
options.c: the item's fair value can be measured reliably and the item is insured against loss
options.d: it is probable that the item will be sold within twelve months and its cost exceeds a set minimum amount

questions.explanation: The two recognition criteria are that future economic benefits are probable and that the cost can be measured reliably. Option A is wrong because an item bought on credit can still be recognised. Option C is wrong because recognition depends on cost, not fair value or insurance, and option D describes something held for sale, which is not PPE.

questions.question: At initial recognition, IAS 16 requires an item of property, plant and equipment to be measured at
questions.explanation: IAS 16 requires PPE to be measured at cost when it is first recognised. Option B can only be used later if the entity chooses the revaluation model. Option D is an inventory measure, and option C is used only in impairment testing.

questions.question: Directly attributable costs that may be included in the cost of PPE are best described as costs that

options.a: are incurred to run the asset after it has been brought into use
options.b: are shared by all departments of the business
options.c: arise from training staff to operate the asset
options.d: would have been avoided if the asset had not been purchased or constructed

questions.explanation: A directly attributable cost exists only because the asset is being bought or built, so it would have been avoided otherwise. Option A describes running costs after the asset is ready for use, which are expensed. Option B describes general overheads, and option C describes training costs, both of which are excluded from cost.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a directly attributable cost of an item of property, plant and equipment?

options.b: Repainting the asset after it has been in use

questions.explanation: Repainting an asset that is already in use is a maintenance cost and is listed among the expenses excluded from the cost of PPE. Site preparation, initial delivery and handling, and installation and assembly (options D, A and C) are all directly attributable costs that are capitalised.

questions.question: How are the expected future costs of dismantling and removing an item of PPE and restoring its site treated at initial recognition?

options.a: They are expensed only when the dismantling actually takes place
options.b: The full undiscounted estimate is included in cost
options.c: The initial estimate is included in cost, discounted to its present value
options.d: They are deducted from the purchase price as a rebate

questions.explanation: The initial estimate of dismantling, removal and site restoration costs forms part of the cost of the asset, and because the cash is paid in future it is discounted to present value. Option B ignores discounting, option A ignores the requirement to include the estimate in cost at the start, and option D confuses it with trade discounts and rebates.

questions.question: Lekki Bottling Ltd finished installing a new bottling line on 1 March and it was capable of operating from that date. Because orders were low, it was not used until 1 June, and it then ran below normal capacity for two months. How should costs incurred after 1 March be treated?

options.a: They are capitalised until the line reaches normal capacity
options.b: They are capitalised until the end of the financial year
options.c: They are expensed, because capitalisation stops when the asset is ready for use
options.d: They are capitalised until 1 June, when the line was first used

questions.explanation: Capitalisation ends when the asset is ready for use, meaning capable of operating as intended by management, even if it is brought into use later. Options D and A are wrong because waiting for first use or for demand to build up does not justify further capitalisation. Option B has no basis in IAS 16.

questions.question: Subsequent expenditure on an item of property, plant and equipment should be capitalised only when it

options.a: enhances the benefits of the asset, such as increasing the revenue it can generate
options.b: is incurred to restore the asset after normal wear and tear
options.c: is larger than the annual depreciation charge on the asset
options.d: is paid for in cash rather than on credit

questions.explanation: Subsequent costs are added to the asset only if they enhance its benefits, for example by extending its life or increasing the revenue it can generate. Option D is irrelevant because the payment method does not decide capitalisation. Option B describes repairs, which are expensed, and option C is not a test used by IAS 16.

questions.question: In simple terms, the main purpose of charging depreciation is to

options.a: build up a cash fund to replace the asset at the end of its life
options.b: match the cost of using a non-current asset with the revenue it generates over its useful life
options.c: show the asset at its current market value each year
options.d: reduce the amount of tax the business pays

questions.explanation: Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset over the periods in which it is used, matching that cost against the revenue the asset helps to earn. Option A is wrong because depreciation is not a cash fund. Option C is wrong because depreciation is an allocation of cost, not a valuation, and option D is not the accounting purpose of depreciation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a cause of depreciation?

options.d: An increase in the market price of similar assets

questions.explanation: A rise in market prices does not reduce an asset's usefulness, so it does not cause depreciation. Physical wear and tear, obsolescence and passage of time (options C, B and A) are all causes of depreciation, along with use, change in technology or fashion, and depletion.

questions.question: An oil company's well in the Niger Delta loses value as crude oil is extracted from it each year. This cause of depreciation is best described as
questions.explanation: Depletion is the cause of depreciation for mineral resources: as the oil is extracted, less remains. Option A applies to items that go out of style, option D applies to assets with a fixed legal or time-based life, and option C applies when an asset is overtaken by newer ones.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a time-based method of depreciation?
questions.explanation: The units of production method charges depreciation based on output, so it is a service-based method. The sum of the digit, sinking fund and annuity methods (options B, D and C) are time-based methods, together with straight line and reducing balance.

questions.question: Under IAS 16, the depreciation method applied to an asset should reflect

options.a: the pattern in which the asset's future economic benefits are expected to be consumed
options.b: the method that gives the lowest charge in the first year
options.c: the method used by the entity's main competitors
options.d: the pattern in which the asset's purchase price was paid

questions.explanation: IAS 16 requires the depreciation method to follow the pattern in which the entity expects to consume the asset's future economic benefits. Options B and C pick a method for convenience or comparison rather than consumption pattern. Option D confuses depreciation with the payment schedule.

questions.question: The depreciation method that charges the same amount every year and is also known as the fixed instalment method is the
questions.explanation: The straight line method divides the depreciable amount equally over the useful life, so each year bears the same charge. Option C charges more in early years, option B varies with output, and option D also gives a falling charge over time.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the reducing balance method of depreciation?

options.a: A fixed rate is applied to the original cost each year, giving the same charge every year
options.b: The depreciable amount is divided equally by the number of years of useful life
options.c: A fixed rate is applied to the carrying amount at the beginning of each year, giving higher charges in early years
options.d: The charge depends on the number of units produced by the asset in each year

questions.explanation: Under reducing balance, a fixed rate is applied to the opening carrying amount, so the charge is highest at the start and falls each year. Options A and B describe the straight line method, which gives an equal charge. Option D describes the units of production method.

questions.question: IAS 16 requires the residual value and useful life of an asset to be reviewed at least at each financial year-end. If expectations differ from previous estimates, the change is accounted for as

options.a: a change in accounting policy, applied retrospectively
options.b: a change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively
options.c: a prior period error, corrected by restating comparatives
options.d: an impairment loss recognised in other comprehensive income

questions.explanation: A revised useful life or residual value is a change in accounting estimate, so it affects the current and future periods only. Options A and C would require restating earlier years, which is wrong because earlier estimates were reasonable when made. Option D confuses a revised estimate with impairment.

questions.question: Under the cost model in IAS 16, after recognition an item of PPE is carried at

options.a: the lower of cost and net realisable value
options.b: fair value at each reporting date with no depreciation
options.c: fair value at the date of revaluation less subsequent depreciation and impairment
options.d: cost less accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment losses

questions.explanation: The cost model keeps the asset at its original cost and deducts accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment losses. Option C describes the revaluation model. Option B is not permitted for PPE, which must still be depreciated, and option A is the inventory rule.

questions.question: Under the revaluation model in IAS 16, an item of PPE whose fair value can be measured reliably is carried at

options.a: its residual value until it is disposed of
options.b: its original cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment losses
options.c: its fair value at the date of revaluation less subsequent accumulated depreciation and impairment losses
options.d: its recoverable amount at each reporting date

questions.explanation: The revaluation model carries the asset at a revalued amount, which is fair value at the revaluation date less any later accumulated depreciation and impairment losses. Option B is the cost model. Option D is used only to measure impairment, and option A confuses carrying amount with residual value.

questions.question: When the carrying amount of an item of PPE is increased as a result of a revaluation (with no previous revaluation decrease), the increase is

options.a: recognised as a liability until the asset is sold
options.b: recognised as revenue in profit or loss
options.c: deducted from accumulated depreciation of other assets
options.d: recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in equity as revaluation surplus

questions.explanation: A revaluation increase goes to other comprehensive income and builds up in equity under the heading revaluation surplus. Option B is wrong because an unrealised gain from revaluation is not revenue. Options C and A have no basis in IAS 16.

questions.question: Benin Foods Ltd decides to revalue one of its factory buildings under the revaluation model. IAS 16 requires that

options.a: all assets of the company, including inventories, are revalued
options.b: only that one building is revalued and the others stay at cost
options.c: the entire class of property, plant and equipment to which that building belongs is revalued
options.d: the building is revalued only if its fair value is below cost

questions.explanation: If an item of PPE is revalued, the whole class to which it belongs must be revalued, which stops entities from picking only favourable items. Option B allows selective revaluation, which is not allowed. Option A goes too far because inventories are not PPE, and option D is wrong because revaluation applies whether fair value rises or falls.

questions.question: An item of property, plant and equipment should be derecognised

options.a: at the end of each financial year and then recognised again
options.b: when its fair value falls below its carrying amount
options.c: on disposal, or when no future economic benefits are expected from its use or disposal
options.d: when it has been fully depreciated, even if it is still in use

questions.explanation: PPE is removed from the statement of financial position when it is disposed of, or when no future economic benefits are expected from using or disposing of it. Option D is wrong because a fully depreciated asset still in use is kept in the records. Option B may indicate impairment but is not derecognition, and option A has no basis.

questions.question: The gain or loss on derecognition of an item of PPE is calculated as the difference between the net disposal proceeds and the carrying amount, and it is

options.a: recognised as revenue from contracts with customers
options.b: added to or deducted from share capital
options.c: recognised in profit or loss, with any gain not classified as revenue

questions.explanation: The gain or loss on disposal goes to profit or loss when the item is derecognised, and IAS 16 says gains are not classified as revenue. Option D is wrong because disposal gains and losses do not go to OCI. Option B has no basis, and option A contradicts the rule that gains are not revenue.

questions.question: Apapa Plastics Ltd bought a moulding machine. Details: list price N6,000,000; import duty N450,000; recoverable VAT N450,000; trade discount N300,000; delivery N120,000; installation N200,000; testing N80,000; staff training N150,000; allocated administration overheads N100,000. What cost should be capitalised?
questions.explanation: Cost = price N6,000,000 + import duty N450,000 - trade discount N300,000 + delivery, installation and testing N400,000 = N6,550,000. Option D wrongly adds the VAT, which is recoverable so it is not part of cost. Option A includes training and administration overheads, which are excluded, and option B forgets to deduct the trade discount.

questions.question: Yaba Logistics Ltd bought a delivery van. Costs: van N3,800,000; registration number N120,000; road licence fee N30,000; delivery charge for the van N45,000; cost of testing the van N60,000; driver's wages for the first year of operation N900,000. What amount should be capitalised as motor vehicle?
questions.explanation: The van, registration, delivery and testing are needed to get the van ready for use: N3,800,000 + N120,000 + N45,000 + N60,000 = N4,025,000. Option D adds the road licence fee, which is a running cost of operating the vehicle. Option B also adds the driver's wages, an operating expense, and option A leaves out registration and testing, which are capitalised.

questions.question: Bonny Offshore Ltd built a drilling platform at a cost of N50,000,000. It must dismantle the platform and restore the site in 10 years, at an estimated cost of N20,000,000. The present value of that estimate is N7,700,000. What is the initial cost of the platform?
questions.explanation: The initial estimate of dismantling and restoration costs is included in cost at its discounted (present) value: N50,000,000 + N7,700,000 = N57,700,000. Option B adds the undiscounted amount, option C ignores the dismantling cost entirely, and option A wrongly deducts it.

questions.question: Agege Foods Ltd built its own storage facility. Costs: building supplies used N4,000,000; employee benefits of staff working directly on the construction N1,500,000; building supplies wasted through an abnormal accident N300,000; site preparation N500,000; general overheads of the company N250,000. What cost should be capitalised?
questions.explanation: Building supplies used, directly related employee benefits and site preparation are capitalised: N4,000,000 + N1,500,000 + N500,000 = N6,000,000. Option C includes the wasted supplies, which are abnormal costs. Option B includes general overheads, which are excluded, and option D includes both.

questions.question: A generator was bought for N3,600,000 with an expected residual value of N400,000 and a useful life of 8 years. What is the annual depreciation under the straight line method?
questions.explanation: Straight line depreciation = (cost - residual value) / useful life = (N3,600,000 - N400,000) / 8 = N400,000. Option B ignores the residual value, option A adds the residual value instead of deducting it, and option D divides by the wrong number of years.

questions.question: A generator cost N3,600,000, has a residual value of N400,000 and a useful life of 8 years. It is depreciated on the straight line basis. What is its carrying amount at the end of year 3?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation is (N3,600,000 - N400,000) / 8 = N400,000, so accumulated depreciation after 3 years is N1,200,000. Carrying amount = N3,600,000 - N1,200,000 = N2,400,000. Option D is the accumulated depreciation, option B ignores the residual value when working out depreciation, and option C wrongly deducts the residual value again.

questions.question: Equipment costing N4,800,000 has an estimated residual value of N300,000 and a useful life of 6 years. Using the straight line method, what is the accumulated depreciation at the end of year 4?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation = (N4,800,000 - N300,000) / 6 = N750,000, so accumulated depreciation after 4 years = N750,000 x 4 = N3,000,000. Option B ignores the residual value, option C is the carrying amount rather than accumulated depreciation, and option A counts only three years.

questions.question: A bus costs N9,000,000 and is expected to have a residual value of N1,500,000 at the end of its useful life of 5 years. What is its depreciable amount?
questions.explanation: Depreciable amount = cost - residual value = N9,000,000 - N1,500,000 = N7,500,000. Option C ignores the residual value, option B adds it, and option D is the annual straight line charge, not the depreciable amount.

questions.question: A machine costing N2,000,000 is depreciated using the reducing balance method at 25% per annum. What is the depreciation charge for year 1?
questions.explanation: In year 1, depreciation = rate x cost = 25% x N2,000,000 = N500,000. Option C is the carrying amount at the end of year 1, option B is the year 2 charge, and option D wrongly spreads the rate as if over four years.

questions.question: A machine costing N2,000,000 is depreciated using the reducing balance method at 25% per annum. What is the depreciation charge for year 2?
questions.explanation: Year 1 depreciation is N500,000, leaving a carrying amount of N1,500,000. Year 2 depreciation = 25% x N1,500,000 = N375,000. Option D applies the rate to cost again (straight line thinking), option B is accumulated depreciation under that same mistake, and option A is the carrying amount at the end of year 2.

questions.question: A machine cost N2,000,000 and is depreciated using the reducing balance method at 25% per annum. What is its carrying amount at the end of year 3?
questions.explanation: Using carrying amount = P(1 - r)^n: N2,000,000 x 0.75^3 = N843,750. Option D deducts 25% of cost each year, which is straight line thinking. Option C is the carrying amount after only two years, and option A is the accumulated depreciation.

questions.question: Ojota Printers Ltd bought a press for N800,000. Its useful life is 4 years and its expected residual value is N192,080. Using R = (1 - nth root of (S/C)) x 100, what is the reducing balance rate?
questions.explanation: S/C = N192,080 / N800,000 = 0.2401, and the 4th root of 0.2401 is 0.7. R = (1 - 0.7) x 100 = 30%. Option C is the straight line charge expressed as a percentage of cost, option D simply divides 100% by four years, and option A forgets to subtract the root from 1.

questions.question: A vehicle that cost N1,250,000 is depreciated at 20% per annum on the reducing balance basis. Using A = P(1 - r)^n, what is its carrying amount at the end of year 3?
questions.explanation: A = N1,250,000 x (1 - 0.2)^3 = N1,250,000 x 0.512 = N640,000. Option A deducts 20% of cost each year, which is the straight line approach. Option B is the carrying amount after two years, and option C is the accumulated depreciation after three years.

questions.question: A bottling machine costs N12,000,000, has a residual value of N2,000,000 and is expected to produce 200,000 crates over its useful life. In year 1 it produced 30,000 crates. Using the units of production method, what is the year 1 depreciation?
questions.explanation: Depreciation per crate = (N12,000,000 - N2,000,000) / 200,000 = N50; year 1 charge = N50 x 30,000 = N1,500,000. Option A ignores the residual value, option D uses an assumed five-year straight line life instead of output, and option C adds the residual value.

questions.question: Machinery that cost N5,000,000 with accumulated depreciation of N3,200,000 was sold for N2,100,000. What is the gain or loss on disposal?
questions.explanation: Carrying amount = N5,000,000 - N3,200,000 = N1,800,000. Proceeds of N2,100,000 exceed that by N300,000, so there is a gain. Option B has the right figure but the wrong direction, option C treats all the proceeds as gain, and option D compares proceeds with cost instead of carrying amount.

questions.question: A truck was bought for N6,000,000 with a residual value of N600,000 and a useful life of 5 years, depreciated on the straight line basis. It was sold at the end of year 3 for N2,500,000. What is the gain or loss on disposal?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation = (N6,000,000 - N600,000) / 5 = N1,080,000; after 3 years accumulated depreciation is N3,240,000 and carrying amount is N2,760,000. Proceeds of N2,500,000 are below that, giving a loss of N260,000. Option D reverses the direction, option A ignores the residual value when calculating depreciation, and option B compares proceeds with cost.

questions.question: Office equipment with a cost of N4,000,000 and accumulated depreciation of N2,500,000 was sold for N1,800,000. Selling costs of N100,000 were paid. What is the gain on disposal?
questions.explanation: Net disposal proceeds = N1,800,000 - N100,000 = N1,700,000; carrying amount = N4,000,000 - N2,500,000 = N1,500,000. Gain = N1,700,000 - N1,500,000 = N200,000. Option A ignores the selling costs, option B treats the net proceeds as the gain, and option C deducts the selling costs twice.

questions.question: Epe Farms Ltd uses the revaluation model for land. Land that cost N20,000,000 was revalued to N26,000,000. There was no previous revaluation. What revaluation surplus is recognised in other comprehensive income?

options.d: Nil, because land is not depreciated

questions.explanation: Revaluation surplus = fair value - carrying amount = N26,000,000 - N20,000,000 = N6,000,000, credited to other comprehensive income. Option B is the new carrying amount, option A is the original cost, and option D is wrong because a surplus arises whenever the revalued amount exceeds carrying amount, depreciated or not.

questions.question: A building with a cost of N10,000,000 and accumulated depreciation of N2,000,000 was revalued to a fair value of N11,000,000. There was no previous revaluation. What is the revaluation surplus?
questions.explanation: Carrying amount before revaluation = N10,000,000 - N2,000,000 = N8,000,000. Surplus = N11,000,000 - N8,000,000 = N3,000,000. Option B compares fair value with cost and ignores depreciation, option A is the new carrying amount, and option D is the old carrying amount.

questions.question: A building carried at N12,000,000 is revalued to N10,500,000. A revaluation surplus of N1,000,000 relating to this building is already held in equity. How much of the decrease is recognised in profit or loss?
questions.explanation: The total decrease is N1,500,000. The first N1,000,000 is debited to other comprehensive income against the existing surplus, and only the remaining N500,000 goes to profit or loss. Option C charges the whole decrease to profit or loss, option D is the part charged to OCI, and option B wrongly assumes the surplus covers the whole decrease.

questions.question: A machine cost N5,000,000 with nil residual value and a useful life of 10 years, depreciated on the straight line basis. At the start of year 5, its remaining useful life is revised to 3 years. What is the depreciation charge for year 5?
questions.explanation: After 4 years the carrying amount is N5,000,000 - (N500,000 x 4) = N3,000,000. As a change in estimate, it is spread over the remaining 3 years: N3,000,000 / 3 = N1,000,000. Option A keeps the old charge, option C spreads the original cost over a revised total life (a retrospective approach), and option B spreads the full cost over the remaining life.

questions.question: A bus has a carrying amount of N2,000,000. During the year the company spent N800,000 on a new engine that extends the bus's useful life and N50,000 on repainting it. Ignoring depreciation for the year, what is the carrying amount of the bus after these costs?
questions.explanation: The engine enhances the bus's benefits by extending its life, so the N800,000 is capitalised, giving N2,000,000 + N800,000 = N2,800,000. The repainting does not increase the bus's revenue-earning capacity, so it is expensed. Option C capitalises the repainting too, option D expenses the engine, and option B capitalises the wrong item.

questions.question: There are two broad approaches to accounting for government grants related to assets: ______, which permits the grant to be recognised outside profit or loss, and the income approach, under which a grant is recognised in profit or loss over one or more periods.
questions.explanation: The capital approach treats a grant as a form of financing, so it is credited outside profit or loss, directly to equity. Option A is actually one way of applying the income approach, where the grant is spread to profit or loss. Options C and B are general bases of accounting, not grant approaches.

questions.question: There are two broad approaches to accounting for government grants related to assets: the capital approach, which permits the grant to be recognised outside profit or loss, and ______, under which a grant is recognised in profit or loss over one or more periods.
questions.explanation: Under the income approach, a grant is recognised in profit or loss over one or more periods, matching it against the costs it is meant to compensate; this is the approach IAS 20 requires. Option D describes taking the grant to equity, which is really the capital approach. Options C and A are measurement ideas for assets, not grant approaches.

questions.question: Government grants shall be recognised in profit or loss on a ______ over the periods in which the entity recognises as expenses the related costs for which the grants are intended to compensate.

options.c: once-off basis in the year of receipt

questions.explanation: IAS 20 requires grants to be recognised in profit or loss on a systematic basis, matched with the costs they are meant to cover. Options D and C would put the grant into profit when the money arrives, which breaks that matching. Option B is too narrow, because the pattern follows the related costs, which need not be straight-line.

questions.question: ______ are grants given to businesses for any purpose other than to support the acquisition of non-current assets.
questions.explanation: Under IAS 20, any grant that is not a grant related to assets is a grant related to income, for example a grant to cover wages or running costs. Option A is the opposite category, given to buy or build non-current assets. Option B is the wider term that includes grants and non-monetary help, and option C is just one possible form a grant can take.

questions.question: In accordance with IAS 20, grants should only be recognised when there is reasonable assurance that ______

options.a: the entity will comply with the conditions attaching to them and the grants will be received
options.b: the grants have been received in cash, even if conditions are not yet met
options.c: the related asset has been fully depreciated
options.d: the entity has made a profit for the year and the grant is material

questions.explanation: IAS 20 sets two conditions that must both hold: reasonable assurance that the entity will comply with the grant's conditions, and that the grant will actually be received. Option B is wrong because receiving cash alone is not enough. Options C and D are not recognition conditions at all.

questions.question: The capital approach to accounting for grants permits the grant to be recognised as ______

options.a: a deduction from the related expense
options.b: income in profit or loss over the useful life of the asset
options.c: a credit directly to shareholders' interests (equity), outside profit or loss

questions.explanation: The capital approach treats a grant as a form of financing, not earned income, so it is credited directly to shareholders' interests in equity and never passes through profit or loss. Option B describes the income approach. Option A is a presentation choice for income-related grants under the income approach, and option D is not how either approach treats the grant.

questions.question: XYZ Nigeria Limited received a grant of N10,000,000 to finance the acquisition of a special model of Micro Magnetic machine used in a specialist hospital. The cost of the machine is N100,000,000. The machine is to be depreciated on a straight-line basis over five years with no residual value. If the grant is deducted from the cost of the asset, what is the annual depreciation charge?
questions.explanation: Deducting the grant gives a net cost of N100,000,000 - N10,000,000 = N90,000,000, and N90,000,000 / 5 = N18,000,000 a year. Option A depreciates the full cost, which is what happens under the deferred income method instead. Option C adds the grant to the cost, and option D is the yearly share of the grant, not the depreciation.

questions.question: XYZ Nigeria Limited received a grant of N10,000,000 to finance the acquisition of a special model of Micro Magnetic machine used in a specialist hospital. The cost of the machine is N100,000,000. The machine is to be depreciated on a straight-line basis over five years with no residual value. If the grant is treated as deferred income, how much of the grant is credited to profit or loss each year?
questions.explanation: Under the deferred income method the machine is depreciated at N100,000,000 / 5 = N20,000,000 a year, and the N10,000,000 grant is released to profit or loss over the same five years at N10,000,000 / 5 = N2,000,000 a year. Option A credits the whole grant in year 1, which ignores matching the grant with the depreciation it helps fund. Option C is the depreciation charge, and option D is the net depreciation under the deduction method.

questions.question: XYZ Nigeria Limited received a grant of N30,000,000 to build an aircraft hangar over a period of five years. The construction cost is estimated to be N20,000,000, which would be incurred over the five years as follows: Year 1 N2,000,000; Year 2 N3,000,000; Year 3 N4,000,000; Year 4 N5,000,000; Year 5 N6,000,000. The grant is to be recognised as income in proportion to each year's construction cost. How much grant income should be recognised in Year 4?
questions.explanation: IAS 20 matches grant income with the related costs, so Year 4 income is (N5,000,000 / N20,000,000) x N30,000,000 = N7,500,000. Option A spreads the grant equally over five years (N30,000,000 / 5) and ignores the cost pattern. Option B is the cost incurred in Year 4, not the grant income, and option D is the cumulative grant income for Years 1 to 4 (N3,000,000 + N4,500,000 + N6,000,000 + N7,500,000).

questions.question: Under IAS 20, the government of nations, government agencies and similar bodies, whether local, national or international, are collectively referred to as
questions.explanation: IAS 20 uses the single word government to cover nations' governments, government agencies and similar bodies at local, national or international level. Option A is an action that gives economic benefits, not the body that gives it. Options D and C are not the defined term used in the standard.

questions.question: For the purpose of IAS 20, which of the following would NOT fall within the meaning of government?

options.d: A privately owned commercial bank lending to the entity

questions.explanation: Government covers the government of nations, government agencies and similar bodies, whether local, national or international. A privately owned commercial bank is not a government body, so its lending is outside IAS 20. Options C, A and B are all expressly within the meaning of government.

questions.question: Government assistance, quantified in monetary terms, in the form of transfers of resources to an entity in return for past or future compliance with certain conditions relating to its operating activities, is called
questions.explanation: A government grant is assistance that has a monetary value and involves a transfer of resources in return for compliance with conditions. Option C and option B describe help with no monetary value, such as a tax holiday, which is assistance but not a grant. Option D is only the account used to hold a grant under one method, not the definition of a grant.

questions.question: A government grant is given to an entity in return for

options.a: Taxes the entity has paid in prior years
options.b: Shares issued by the entity to the government
options.c: Past or future compliance with certain conditions relating to the entity's operating activities
options.d: The entity agreeing to become a government agency

questions.explanation: A grant is a transfer of resources in return for past or future compliance with conditions relating to the entity's operating activities. Option B would make the government an investor, not a grantor. Options A and D are not conditions linked to the entity's operating activities.

questions.question: Any action of the government aimed at giving economic benefits to an entity or range of entities qualifying under certain criteria is known as
questions.explanation: Government assistance is the broad term for any government action that gives economic benefits to qualifying entities, and it includes grants. Options A and B are the two narrower types of grant, which must involve a transfer of resources with a monetary value. Option D is an accounting balance, not a government action.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about government grants and government assistance is correct?

options.a: Government assistance must always have a monetary value placed on it
options.b: All government grants are assistance, but not all assistance is a grant
options.c: All government assistance is a grant, but not all grants are assistance
options.d: Government grants and government assistance mean exactly the same thing

questions.explanation: Grants are the part of government assistance that has a monetary value, so every grant is assistance but some assistance, like a tax holiday, is not a grant. Option C reverses the relationship. Options D and A are wrong because assistance can exist without any monetary value.

questions.question: The Federal Government grants Ikeja Foods Ltd a five-year tax holiday under a pioneer status scheme, with no cash transferred. Under IAS 20, this is best described as

options.a: Government assistance without monetary value, not a government grant
options.b: A government grant related to assets
options.c: A government grant related to income
options.d: A government grant to be credited to deferred income

questions.explanation: A tax holiday is a classic example of government assistance that has no monetary value placed on it, so it is not a grant. Options B, C and D all treat it as a grant, but a grant requires a transfer of resources quantified in monetary terms.

questions.question: What distinguishes a government grant from other forms of government assistance?

options.a: It involves a transfer of resources with a monetary value placed on it
options.b: It is given only to government-owned companies
options.c: It is always recognised directly in equity

questions.explanation: Grants have monetary values placed on them and involve a transfer of money or resources, which is why they must be accounted for. Option D is wrong because grants are given in return for compliance with conditions. Options B and C are not features of a grant at all.

questions.question: Grants given to businesses with the general condition that they purchase or construct non-current assets are called
questions.explanation: Grants related to assets carry the condition that the entity buys or builds non-current assets. Option C covers grants for any purpose other than acquiring non-current assets. Option B is help without a monetary value, such as a tax holiday, and option A is not one of the two types of grant.

questions.question: Grants related to income are best described as grants given to businesses

options.a: For any purpose other than to support the acquisition of non-current assets
options.b: Only after the related asset has been fully depreciated
options.c: Only to purchase or construct non-current assets
options.d: Only in the form of tax holidays

questions.explanation: Grants related to income are all grants other than those given to support the acquisition of non-current assets. Option C describes grants related to assets. Option D is wrong because a tax holiday is not a grant at all, and option B is not part of the definition.

questions.question: The Lagos State Government pays N40 million to Ota Clinics Ltd on condition that it buys a new dialysis machine. This grant is

options.c: Not a grant because it is from a state, not federal, government

questions.explanation: The grant defrays the cost of acquiring a non-current asset, which makes it a grant related to assets. Option D applies to grants for purposes other than acquiring non-current assets. Option C is wrong because government includes local and state-level authorities, and option B fails because cash with a monetary value was transferred.

questions.question: A government agency gives Kano Textiles Ltd N15 million to cover part of its staff wage costs for the next two years. No asset purchase is required. This is

options.c: A capital contribution by the government

questions.explanation: Since the money is not given to acquire non-current assets, it is a grant related to income and will be matched against the wage costs it compensates. Option B requires a condition to buy or build non-current assets. Option A fails because cash was transferred, and option C would make the government an owner, which is not the case.

questions.question: Enugu Agro Ltd has been told it will receive a N20 million grant from a state agency, and it is reasonably assured the cash will be paid. However, it is not yet reasonably assured that it can meet the job-creation condition attached. How should the grant be treated now?

options.a: It should be recognised as deferred income immediately
options.b: It should be recognised in full as income immediately
options.c: It should not be recognised until both conditions are met
options.d: It should be deducted from the cost of its assets immediately

questions.explanation: A grant is recognised only when there is reasonable assurance both that the conditions will be met and that the grant will be received. Here only one condition is satisfied, so nothing is recognised yet. Options B, A and D all recognise the grant in some form too early.

questions.question: When a grant related to an asset is written off against the cost of the non-current asset, depreciation is based on

options.a: The amount of the grant only
options.b: The cost of the asset reduced by the grant
options.c: The full cost of the asset before the grant
options.d: The fair value of the asset at year end

questions.explanation: Deducting the grant from cost reduces the asset's value, and depreciation is then charged on that reduced amount. Option C applies to the deferred income method, where depreciation is on the full cost. Options A and D are not bases used for depreciation here.

questions.question: Under the deferred income method for a grant related to an asset, which of the following is correct?

options.a: The grant is credited to the asset account and the asset is depreciated on the net amount
options.b: Depreciation is based on the full cost, and a portion of the grant is transferred to income each year
options.c: Depreciation is based on cost less grant, and nothing is transferred to income
options.d: The whole grant is taken to income in the year of receipt

questions.explanation: With the deferred income method, the asset stays at full cost and is depreciated on that amount, while part of the deferred grant is released to the income statement each year to offset the higher depreciation. Options C and A describe deducting the grant from the asset's cost. Option D ignores the systematic matching of grant income with depreciation.

questions.question: Which method of accounting for a grant related to an asset shows the asset in the statement of financial position at its full cost and shows the unreleased grant as a separate balance?

options.a: The method of deducting the grant from the cost of the asset
options.c: Treating the grant as government assistance without monetary value
options.d: Recognising the grant as income on receipt

questions.explanation: The deferred income method leaves the asset at its full cost and carries the unreleased grant in a deferred income account. Option A reduces the asset's carrying amount by the grant, so no separate grant balance remains. Options D and C are not acceptable treatments for a grant related to an asset.

questions.question: When a grant related to an asset is deducted from the cost of the asset, the grant received is recorded as

options.a: A debit to the asset (machine) account
options.b: A credit to the asset (machine) account
options.c: A credit to a deferred income account

questions.explanation: Deducting the grant from cost means the grant cash is credited to the machine account, which reduces the asset's balance. Option A would increase the asset instead. Option C is the deferred income method, and option D treats the government as a shareholder.

questions.question: Under the deferred income method, the yearly portion of a grant related to an asset is transferred by debiting deferred income and crediting
questions.explanation: Each year part of the deferred grant is released to the income statement, where it offsets the depreciation charge. Option C is the treatment when the grant is deducted from cost. Options A and B are not where the yearly release goes.

questions.question: How are grants related to income treated when the cash is received?

options.a: They are recognised as income in full immediately upon receipt
options.b: They are credited directly to retained earnings
options.c: They are not recognised as income immediately; they are matched against the related expense
options.d: They are deducted from the cost of non-current assets

questions.explanation: Grants related to income are recognised in the income statement, matched against the expenses they are meant to cover, so they are not income just because the money has arrived. Option A ignores this matching. Option D is for grants related to assets, and option B bypasses profit or loss altogether.

questions.question: IAS 20 permits grants related to income to be presented either

options.a: In other comprehensive income or directly in equity
options.b: As deferred tax or as a provision
options.c: As a reduction of the cost of non-current assets or as share capital
options.d: Separately as other income or as a reduction of the related expense

questions.explanation: Income-related grants are shown either separately as other income or deducted from the related expense. Option C mixes up the asset-grant treatment with share capital. Options B and A are not presentation choices for income-related grants.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an acceptable way to present a grant related to income?

options.a: Crediting it directly to equity when received
options.b: Showing it separately as other income
options.c: Deducting it from the related expense
options.d: Recognising it in the income statement as the related costs are incurred

questions.explanation: Grants related to income go through the income statement, matched against the expenses they compensate, so crediting them straight to equity is not acceptable. Options B and C are the two permitted presentation choices, and option D describes the required matching.

questions.question: In allocating a grant related to income over years of construction, the step of dividing each year's cost by the total cost and multiplying by the grant value is called

options.a: Ascertaining the total value of the grant
options.c: Prorating the grant using each year's estimated cost
options.d: Writing off the grant against the cost of the asset

questions.explanation: Prorating means sharing the grant in proportion to each year's cost, that is (year's cost / total cost) x grant. Options B and A are the earlier steps that supply the figures for this calculation. Option D is a method for grants related to assets, not this allocation.

questions.question: Sokoto Mills Ltd buys a machine for N60,000,000 and receives a government grant of N12,000,000 towards it. The machine is depreciated straight-line over 6 years. If the grant is deducted from the cost of the machine, the annual depreciation charge is
questions.explanation: Deducting the grant gives a net cost of N60,000,000 - N12,000,000 = N48,000,000, and N48,000,000 / 6 = N8,000,000 a year. Option C depreciates the full cost, which is done only under the deferred income method. Option D spreads only the grant, and option A wrongly adds the grant to cost.

questions.question: Abeokuta Diagnostics Ltd buys a scanner for N80,000,000 and receives a grant of N20,000,000 towards it. The scanner is depreciated straight-line over 5 years. Using the method that deducts the grant from the cost of the asset, what is the carrying amount of the scanner at the end of year 2?
questions.explanation: Net cost is N80,000,000 - N20,000,000 = N60,000,000, depreciated at N12,000,000 a year, so after 2 years the carrying amount is N60,000,000 - N24,000,000 = N36,000,000. Option A ignores the grant and depreciates the full cost. Option D is the net cost before any depreciation, and option C subtracts two years of depreciation from the full cost but forgets to deduct the grant itself.

questions.question: Ilorin Dairy Ltd receives a government grant of N18,000,000 towards a cold room costing N75,000,000, depreciated straight-line over 5 years. Under the deferred income method, how much of the grant is transferred to the income statement each year?
questions.explanation: The grant is released in line with the asset's 5-year life: N18,000,000 / 5 = N3,600,000 a year. Option A is the yearly depreciation on full cost, not the grant release. Option B is depreciation on cost less grant, used when the grant is deducted from cost, and option D recognises the whole grant at once.

questions.question: Owerri Bottling Ltd received a grant of N24,000,000 for a bottling line depreciated straight-line over 6 years, and uses the deferred income method. What is the balance on the deferred income account at the end of year 3?
questions.explanation: The annual release is N24,000,000 / 6 = N4,000,000, so after 3 years N12,000,000 has been released and N12,000,000 remains as deferred income. Option D deducts only 2 years of release. Option B is just one year's release, not the balance remaining, and option C ignores the releases entirely.

questions.question: Port Harcourt Marine Ltd buys a vessel engine for N60,000,000 with the help of a N10,000,000 grant. The engine is depreciated straight-line over 5 years and the deferred income method is used. What is the carrying amount of the engine at the end of year 2?
questions.explanation: Under the deferred income method the engine stays at full cost, depreciated at N60,000,000 / 5 = N12,000,000 a year, so after 2 years it is carried at N36,000,000. Option B is the answer if the grant had been deducted from cost, which is the other method. Option C is cost less grant with no depreciation, and option A charges only one year.

questions.question: Jos Agro Ltd buys a tractor for N45,000,000 with a N9,000,000 government grant. The tractor is depreciated straight-line over 3 years and the deferred income method is used. What is the net charge to profit or loss each year (depreciation less grant income)?
questions.explanation: Depreciation on full cost is N45,000,000 / 3 = N15,000,000 and the grant released is N9,000,000 / 3 = N3,000,000, so the net charge is N12,000,000. Option B ignores the grant income. Option D is only the grant release, and option C wrongly adds the grant income to depreciation.

questions.question: Kaduna Steel Ltd buys a furnace for N72,000,000 and receives a grant of N18,000,000 towards it. Using the deferred income method, with straight-line depreciation over 4 years, what is the annual depreciation charge?
questions.explanation: Under the deferred income method, depreciation is based on the full cost: N72,000,000 / 4 = N18,000,000. Option A depreciates cost less grant, which is the method that deducts the grant from cost. Option C is the yearly grant release, not depreciation, and option D wrongly adds the grant to cost.

questions.question: Akure Printing Ltd buys a press for N35,000,000 and receives a N7,000,000 grant towards it. If the grant is deducted from the cost of the asset, what balance is carried down on the press account immediately after recording the grant (before any depreciation)?
questions.explanation: The grant is credited to the press account, so the balance carried down is N35,000,000 - N7,000,000 = N28,000,000. Option B is the balance under the deferred income method, where the asset stays at full cost. Option D adds the grant instead of deducting it, and option A is the grant alone.

questions.question: Calabar Foods Ltd receives a grant of N8,000,000 for equipment depreciated straight-line over 4 years and uses the deferred income method. What deferred income balance appears in the statement of financial position at the end of year 1?
questions.explanation: N8,000,000 / 4 = N2,000,000 is released in year 1, leaving N6,000,000 as deferred income. Option B ignores the year 1 release. Option A is the amount released, not the balance remaining, and option D deducts two years of release.

questions.question: Benin Plastics Ltd buys a moulding machine for N90,000,000 with a N30,000,000 grant, depreciated straight-line over 5 years. If the grant is deducted from cost, what is the TOTAL depreciation charged over the machine's whole life?
questions.explanation: When the grant is deducted from cost, only the net cost of N90,000,000 - N30,000,000 = N60,000,000 is depreciated over the 5 years. Option A is the total depreciation under the deferred income method. Option B is the grant itself, and option D wrongly adds the grant to the cost.

questions.question: Warri Fabrication Ltd received a N12,500,000 grant for a crane depreciated straight-line over 5 years and uses the deferred income method. What is the deferred income balance at the end of year 4?
questions.explanation: The annual release is N12,500,000 / 5 = N2,500,000, so after 4 years N10,000,000 has been released and N2,500,000 remains for year 5. Option C deducts only 3 years. Option A is the total released so far, not the balance, and option B would apply only at the end of year 5.

questions.question: Asaba Pharma Ltd buys a production line for N120,000,000 with a N24,000,000 grant, depreciated straight-line over 8 years. What is the net annual effect on profit (expense) under EACH method?

options.a: N12,000,000 if deducted from cost; N18,000,000 under deferred income
options.b: N12,000,000 if deducted from cost; N15,000,000 under deferred income

questions.explanation: Deducting the grant gives depreciation of N96,000,000 / 8 = N12,000,000, while the deferred income method charges N15,000,000 depreciation less N3,000,000 grant income, also N12,000,000. Option B forgets to offset the grant income under the deferred income method. Option D ignores the grant completely, and option A adds the grant income to depreciation instead of offsetting it.

questions.question: Ibadan Builders Ltd receives a N18,000,000 government grant related to a four-year construction project. Estimated costs are: Year 1 N2,000,000; Year 2 N3,000,000; Year 3 N4,000,000; Year 4 N3,000,000. Prorating the grant on each year's cost, how much grant income is recognised in Year 3?
questions.explanation: Total cost is N12,000,000, so Year 3 income is (N4,000,000 / N12,000,000) x N18,000,000 = N6,000,000. Option B spreads the grant equally over 4 years instead of in line with the costs. Option C is the Year 3 cost itself, and option D inverts the ratio by dividing the cost by the grant.

questions.question: Ibadan Builders Ltd receives a N18,000,000 government grant related to a four-year construction project, with estimated costs of Year 1 N2,000,000, Year 2 N3,000,000, Year 3 N4,000,000 and Year 4 N3,000,000. Prorating the grant on each year's cost, how much grant income is recognised in Year 1?
questions.explanation: Year 1 income is (N2,000,000 / N12,000,000) x N18,000,000 = N3,000,000. Option D is just the Year 1 cost, not a share of the grant. Option A is an equal split over 4 years, which ignores the cost pattern, and option C wrongly subtracts the cost from the grant.

questions.question: Yola Hangars Ltd receives a N24,000,000 grant related to a five-year construction programme with estimated costs of: Year 1 N1,000,000; Year 2 N2,500,000; Year 3 N3,500,000; Year 4 N4,000,000; Year 5 N5,000,000. Prorating the grant on each year's cost, how much grant income is recognised in Year 5?
questions.explanation: Total cost is N16,000,000, so Year 5 income is (N5,000,000 / N16,000,000) x N24,000,000 = N7,500,000. Option C is an equal yearly split that ignores the cost pattern. Option A is the Year 5 cost, and option B is simply the grant minus total cost, which has no meaning here.

questions.question: Yola Hangars Ltd receives a N24,000,000 grant related to a five-year construction programme with total estimated costs of N16,000,000. The grant is prorated on each year's cost. What TOTAL grant income is recognised over the five-year period?
questions.explanation: Prorating shares out the whole grant across the years in proportion to cost, so the yearly amounts add up to the full grant of N24,000,000, even though it is more than the total cost. Option A is the total cost, not the grant income. Options C and B combine grant and cost in ways the method never uses.

questions.question: Yola Hangars Ltd receives a N24,000,000 grant related to a five-year construction programme with estimated costs of: Year 1 N1,000,000; Year 2 N2,500,000; Year 3 N3,500,000; Year 4 N4,000,000; Year 5 N5,000,000. Prorating the grant on each year's cost, what is the cumulative grant income recognised by the end of Year 2?
questions.explanation: Year 1 income is N1,500,000 and Year 2 income is N3,750,000 (each year's cost / N16,000,000 x N24,000,000), giving N5,250,000 in total. Option B uses an equal split over 5 years. Option C is the cumulative cost, not grant income, and option A is the Year 2 amount alone.

questions.question: IAS 23 focuses on ______

options.c: accounting for revenue from contracts with customers

questions.explanation: IAS 23 Borrowing Costs sets out when borrowing costs are capitalised as part of a qualifying asset and when they are expensed. Option B is IAS 20. Option D is IAS 2, and option C is IFRS 15.

questions.question: Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition or construction of a "qualifying asset" must be ______ according to IAS 23 on borrowing costs.

options.b: expensed in profit or loss as incurred
options.d: capitalised as part of the cost of that asset

questions.explanation: IAS 23 requires borrowing costs that are directly attributable to a qualifying asset to be capitalised as part of the asset's cost. Option B is how other borrowing costs are treated, and IAS 23 does not allow it for qualifying assets. Options A and C are not treatments of borrowing costs at all.

questions.question: ______ and ______ are components of borrowing costs.

options.a: Interest expense calculated using the effective interest method, and finance charges on leases
options.b: Dividends paid on ordinary shares, and share issue costs
options.c: Depreciation of the qualifying asset, and repairs
options.d: Income tax expense, and audit fees

questions.explanation: IAS 23 describes borrowing costs as interest and other costs of borrowing funds, including interest expense under the effective interest method and interest on lease liabilities. Option B relates to equity, not borrowing. Options C and D are ordinary operating or tax costs with nothing to do with borrowing.

questions.question: Platinum Nigeria Limited (year ended 31 December 2024) has the following general borrowings, all outstanding for the whole year: 10% Bank Loan N10,000,000; 5% Debenture Loan N20,000,000; 20% Bank Loan N50,000,000. It used these general borrowings to finance construction of its tech city, a qualifying asset. Construction started on 1 April 2024, when N10,000,000 was spent, and a further N40,000,000 was spent on 1 June 2024. Under IAS 23, what capitalisation rate should be applied to the expenditure?

options.a: 5%, the lowest rate on the borrowings
options.c: 15%, the weighted average rate on the general borrowings (N12,000,000 / N80,000,000)
options.d: 20%, the highest rate on the borrowings

questions.explanation: For general borrowings, IAS 23 uses a capitalisation rate equal to the weighted average of the borrowing costs on those loans. Total interest is N1,000,000 + N1,000,000 + N10,000,000 = N12,000,000 on borrowings of N80,000,000, so the rate is 15%. Option B ignores the size of each loan, while options D and A pick a single loan's rate with no basis.

questions.question: Platinum Nigeria Limited (year ended 31 December 2024) has the following general borrowings, all outstanding for the whole year: 10% Bank Loan N10,000,000; 5% Debenture Loan N20,000,000; 20% Bank Loan N50,000,000. It used these general borrowings to finance construction of its tech city, a qualifying asset. Construction started on 1 April 2024, when N10,000,000 was spent, and a further N40,000,000 was spent on 1 June 2024. Using a capitalisation rate of 15%, how much borrowing cost should be capitalised for 2024?
questions.explanation: Capitalisation starts when each amount is spent: N10,000,000 x 15% x 9/12 = N1,125,000 (April to December) plus N40,000,000 x 15% x 7/12 = N3,500,000 (June to December), a total of N4,625,000. The rest of the N12,000,000 total interest, N7,375,000, is expensed, which is option D. Option A charges a full year on the N50,000,000, and option C charges the N40,000,000 for nine months instead of seven.

questions.question: The inclusion of management fee and service charges are what types of borrowing costs?
questions.explanation: Management fees and service charges paid to arrange a loan are ancillary costs - extra costs incurred in connection with arranging the borrowing, on top of the interest itself. Option A is wrong because interest is the charge for using the money, not the fees for setting up the loan. Option D, inflation, is not a borrowing cost at all.

questions.question: For the purpose of capitalising borrowing costs under IAS 23, borrowings are divided into how many types?
questions.explanation: For capitalising borrowing costs, IAS 23 distinguishes two types of borrowing: specific borrowings taken out to finance a particular qualifying asset, and general borrowings used for several purposes. The other options do not match these two categories.

questions.question: When loans are taken from more than one source with different rates, the method recommended by IAS in computing the interest rate is....
questions.explanation: When an entity has general borrowings from several lenders at different rates, IAS 23 requires a capitalisation rate equal to the weighted average of the borrowing costs on those general borrowings. Option A, the effective interest method, is how interest on each individual loan is measured, not how the rate across several loans is combined. Options C and D are not methods used under IAS 23.

questions.question: Interest and other costs that an entity incurs in connection with the borrowing of funds are called
questions.explanation: Borrowing costs are interest and other costs an entity incurs in connection with borrowing funds. Option A is a broader term for costs of acquiring or issuing financial instruments, option C is a general phrase used for costs of bringing assets into use, and option D is only one possible source of borrowing costs, namely the finance charge element.

questions.question: An asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale is called

options.b: A non-current asset held for sale

questions.explanation: A qualifying asset is one that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale, and only such assets attract capitalised borrowing costs. Option B is an asset whose carrying amount will be recovered mainly through sale, option D may or may not be a qualifying asset depending on how long it takes to get ready, and option A is a general classification, not the IAS 23 term.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of borrowing costs under IAS 23?

options.a: Interest in respect of lease liabilities
options.b: Interest expense calculated using the effective interest method
options.d: Exchange differences on foreign currency borrowings to the extent regarded as an adjustment to interest costs

questions.explanation: Dividends are distributions to owners from equity, so they are not costs of borrowing funds. Options A, B and D are the items that IAS 23 lists as possible components of borrowing costs.

questions.question: Which of the following is most likely to be a qualifying asset under IAS 23?

options.a: Machinery that is ready for use when it is purchased
options.c: A power generation plant that takes two years to construct
options.d: Inventories manufactured in large quantities over a short period

questions.explanation: A power plant that takes a long time to build necessarily takes a substantial period to get ready for use, so it is a qualifying asset. Option D describes inventories made over a short period, option B is specifically stated not to be a qualifying asset, and option A is ready for its intended use when acquired, so none of these qualify.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a qualifying asset under IAS 23?

options.a: A toll bridge being built over several years
options.b: A delivery van bought ready for use from a dealer
options.c: An office complex under construction for two years
options.d: A refinery under construction for the entity's own use

questions.explanation: Assets that are ready for their intended use or sale when acquired are not qualifying assets, so a van bought ready for use attracts no capitalised borrowing costs. Options C, A and D are major construction projects that necessarily take a substantial period of time to get ready, which makes them qualifying assets.

questions.question: Lagos Breweries Ltd borrows to finance its routine production of bottled drinks, which are produced in large quantities on a repetitive basis within a few days. Are these drinks qualifying assets?

options.a: Yes, because the entity borrowed money to produce them
options.b: No, because inventories produced over a short period of time are not qualifying assets
options.c: Yes, because all inventories are qualifying assets
options.d: No, because inventories can never be qualifying assets

questions.explanation: Inventories manufactured over a short period of time do not necessarily take a substantial period to get ready for sale, so they are not qualifying assets. Option C is wrong because only inventories that take a substantial period, such as maturing products, can qualify. Option A confuses the source of finance with the nature of the asset, and option D is too absolute because some inventories can be qualifying assets.

questions.question: How should borrowing costs that are NOT directly attributable to a qualifying asset be treated under IAS 23?

options.b: Deferred and amortised over the term of the loan
options.c: Capitalised as part of the cost of property, plant and equipment
options.d: Recognised as an expense in the period in which they are incurred

questions.explanation: Only borrowing costs directly attributable to a qualifying asset are capitalised; all other borrowing costs are expensed in the period they are incurred. Option C would capitalise costs that do not relate to a qualifying asset, option B delays an expense that belongs to the current period, and option A bypasses profit or loss.

questions.question: Borrowing costs are directly attributable to a qualifying asset when

options.a: They are paid in cash during the year
options.b: They are higher than the market rate of interest
options.c: They would have been avoided if the expenditure on the qualifying asset had not been made
options.d: They relate to any loan taken by the entity during the year

questions.explanation: Directly attributable borrowing costs are those that would have been avoided if the expenditure on the qualifying asset had not been made. Option A is about timing of payment, which is irrelevant, option D is too wide because loans may have nothing to do with the asset, and option B confuses the level of the rate with whether the cost relates to the asset.

questions.question: When an entity borrows funds specifically to obtain a qualifying asset, the amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation is

options.a: The actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing during the period less any investment income on the temporary investment of those borrowings
options.b: The weighted average rate applied to all the entity's borrowings
options.c: The interest that would have been paid at the central bank rate
options.d: The actual borrowing costs incurred plus any investment income on temporary investment

questions.explanation: For specific borrowings, the capitalised amount is the actual borrowing costs incurred during the period less any investment income earned by temporarily investing the unused funds.
