Option D adds the income instead of deducting it. Option B is the method for general borrowings, and option C is not a basis in IAS 23.

questions.question: Abuja Estates Ltd took a N100 million loan at 12% per annum specifically to build an office tower. Construction ran throughout the year. Before the funds were spent, the company temporarily invested part of the loan and earned N2 million. How much borrowing cost should be capitalised for the year?
questions.explanation: Actual interest is N100 million x 12% = N12 million, and the N2 million investment income is deducted, so N10 million is capitalised. Option C ignores the investment income, option B adds the income instead of deducting it, and option A capitalises only the income.

questions.question: Port Harcourt Marine Ltd borrowed N80 million at 12% per annum at the start of the year specifically to build a jetty. Expenditure on the jetty and construction activities both began at the start of month 4, and work continued to the end of the year. Ignoring investment income, how much interest is capitalised for the year?
questions.explanation: Capitalisation begins only when all the commencement conditions are met, so 9 months of interest is capitalised: N80 million x 12% x 9/12 = N7.2 million. Option B capitalises the full year including the 3 months before activities started, and option A is the 3 months of interest that must be expensed. Option C wrongly uses 10 months.

questions.question: When funds are borrowed generally and used to obtain a qualifying asset, how is the amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation determined?

options.a: By applying a capitalisation rate to the expenditures on that asset
options.b: By capitalising all interest incurred by the entity during the year
options.c: By taking the actual interest on the single largest loan
options.d: By applying the central bank's lending rate to the asset's cost

questions.explanation: For general borrowings, the entity applies a capitalisation rate to the expenditures on the qualifying asset. Option C picks an arbitrary loan, option B ignores the limit that capitalised costs relate only to the asset's expenditure, and option D uses an external rate rather than the entity's own borrowing costs.

questions.question: Under IAS 23, the capitalisation rate applied to expenditures on a qualifying asset financed from general borrowings is

options.a: The weighted average of the borrowing costs applicable to the entity's general borrowings outstanding during the period
options.b: The highest interest rate on any of the entity's borrowings
options.c: The rate on the borrowing taken specifically for the asset
options.d: The simple average of the interest rates on all loans regardless of size

questions.explanation: The capitalisation rate is the weighted average of the borrowing costs on the entity's general borrowings outstanding during the period, excluding borrowings made specifically for a qualifying asset. Option B overstates the cost, option D ignores the size of each loan, and option C belongs to the specific borrowings method.

questions.question: Kaduna Steel Ltd had two general loans outstanding throughout the year: N200 million at 10% and N300 million at 15%. What is the capitalisation rate for general borrowings?
questions.explanation: Total interest is N20 million + N45 million = N65 million on N500 million of borrowings, giving a weighted average rate of 13%. Option B is a simple average of the two rates that ignores loan sizes. Option A uses only the higher rate, and option C weights the rates the wrong way round.

questions.question: Kaduna Steel Ltd uses a capitalisation rate of 13% for its general borrowings. On a factory under construction all year, it spent N50 million at the start of the year and a further N40 million exactly halfway through the year. What amount of borrowing costs is capitalised for the year?
questions.explanation: Weighted expenditure is N50 million for 12 months plus N40 million for 6 months, so capitalised cost is N6.5 million + N2.6 million = N9.1 million. Option D applies 13% to N90 million for the full year, ignoring when the second payment was made. Option A ignores the second payment, and option B applies the rate only to the second payment for a full year.

questions.question: Benin Builders Ltd has general borrowings on which it incurred total interest of N65 million in the year. Applying its capitalisation rate to the weighted expenditure on a qualifying asset gives N78 million. How much may be capitalised?
questions.explanation: The amount of borrowing costs capitalised in a period cannot exceed the borrowing costs actually incurred in that period, so capitalisation is limited to N65 million. Option D exceeds the interest actually incurred. Option C is the excess, which is not a capitalised amount, and option B adds the two figures together.

questions.question: When measuring expenditures on a qualifying asset for capitalisation purposes, which of the following is deducted?

options.c: Progress payments received and grants received in connection with the asset

questions.explanation: Expenditures on a qualifying asset include only payments of cash, transfers of other assets or the assumption of interest-bearing liabilities, and they are reduced by any progress payments and grants received for the asset. Options D and A have nothing to do with the asset's expenditure. Option B is a borrowing cost itself, not a deduction from expenditure.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the conditions that must all be met before an entity begins capitalising borrowing costs?

options.a: The entity undertakes activities necessary to prepare the asset for its intended use or sale
options.c: The entity incurs expenditures for the asset
options.d: The asset has been approved for use by a regulator

questions.explanation: Capitalisation begins when the entity first meets all three conditions: it incurs expenditures for the asset, incurs borrowing costs, and undertakes the activities needed to prepare the asset. Regulatory approval is not one of those conditions. Options C, B and A are the three commencement conditions themselves.

questions.question: Owerri Hotels Ltd bought land and took a loan to build a hotel on it, but it is holding the land with no development activity while it waits for a better market. What is the treatment of borrowing costs during this holding period?

options.a: They are capitalised, because borrowing costs are being incurred
options.b: They are capitalised, because expenditure has been incurred on the land
options.c: They are not capitalised, because activities necessary to prepare the asset are not being undertaken
options.d: They are capitalised as part of the cost of the land only

questions.explanation: Merely holding an asset when no production or development is taking place does not qualify, so borrowing costs incurred while land is simply held are not capitalised. Options B and A each rely on just one of the three conditions, but all three must be met together. Option D is wrong for the same reason.

questions.question: Which of the following counts as an activity necessary to prepare an asset for its intended use, so that capitalisation can begin?

options.a: Technical and administrative work before physical construction, such as obtaining permits
options.b: Advertising the finished building to future tenants
options.c: Simply holding the land while no development takes place
options.d: Paying the annual insurance on head office

questions.explanation: Activities necessary to prepare an asset include more than physical construction; they also cover technical and administrative work beforehand, such as obtaining permits. Option C is holding the asset with no development, which does not count. Options B and D are marketing and general administrative costs unrelated to getting the asset ready.

questions.question: When should an entity suspend the capitalisation of borrowing costs on a qualifying asset?

options.a: During extended periods in which it suspends active development of the asset
options.b: While substantial technical and administrative work is being carried out
options.c: Whenever interest rates rise during construction
options.d: During any temporary delay that is a necessary part of the process

questions.explanation: Capitalisation is suspended during extended periods in which active development of the qualifying asset is suspended. Option D is wrong because temporary delays that are a necessary part of the process do not cause suspension. Option B is still active work on the asset, and option C has nothing to do with whether development is continuing.

questions.question: Construction of a bridge in the Niger Delta is held up for some weeks each year because high water levels are common in the region during that season. How are borrowing costs treated during these weeks?

options.a: Capitalisation ceases permanently because the asset is substantially complete
options.b: Capitalisation continues because the delay is a normal, necessary part of the process
options.c: Capitalisation is suspended because no physical work is taking place
options.d: The borrowing costs are written off as an impairment loss

questions.explanation: A temporary delay that is a necessary part of the process, such as high water levels that are common in the region, does not cause capitalisation to be suspended. Option C applies only to extended periods of suspended development that are not part of the normal process. Option A is wrong because the bridge is not complete, and option D has no basis in IAS 23.

questions.question: Jos Mining Ltd borrowed N60 million at 10% per annum specifically to build a processing plant. Construction ran for the whole year except for a 3-month period when the company deliberately halted all development because of a dispute with its contractor. This halt was not a necessary part of the process. How much interest is capitalised for the year?
questions.explanation: Capitalisation is suspended during the 3-month extended halt, so only 9 months is capitalised: N60 million x 10% x 9/12 = N4.5 million, and the remaining N1.5 million is expensed. Option C capitalises the full year, ignoring the suspension. Option A is the amount expensed, and option B wrongly suspends for 6 months.

questions.question: When should an entity cease capitalising borrowing costs on a qualifying asset?

options.a: When the asset is first actually used or sold
options.b: When substantially all the activities necessary to prepare the asset for its intended use or sale are complete
options.c: When all decoration requested by the buyer has been finished
options.d: When the loan used to finance it is fully repaid

questions.explanation: Capitalisation ceases when substantially all the activities needed to prepare the asset for its intended use or sale are complete. Option A waits for actual use, which may come later than readiness. Option D ties cessation to the loan rather than the asset, and option C is wrong because minor outstanding work such as decoration does not keep capitalisation going.

questions.question: Construction of an apartment block by Ajah Homes Ltd is physically complete, and the only remaining work is minor decoration to suit each buyer's specification. What is the status of borrowing cost capitalisation?

options.a: It should continue until the loan is repaid
options.b: It should continue until the decoration is finished
options.c: It should be suspended and restarted after decoration
options.d: It should cease, because substantially all the activities are complete

questions.explanation: An asset is normally ready for its intended use or sale when physical construction is complete, even if minor modifications such as decoration to a buyer's specification are still outstanding. Option B keeps capitalising for minor work, option A wrongly links cessation to the loan, and option C treats completion as a temporary suspension.

questions.question: An entity is building a business park made up of several buildings, each of which can be used on its own while construction continues on the others. When does capitalisation stop for a finished building?

options.a: Only when the whole business park is complete
options.b: When substantially all the activities needed to prepare that building for use are complete
options.c: When the first tenant signs a lease for the park
options.d: At the end of the financial year in which construction began

questions.explanation: Where an asset is completed in parts and each part can be used while work continues on others, capitalisation ceases for each part when substantially all the activities to prepare that part are complete. Option A applies to assets such as an industrial plant whose parts cannot be used separately. Options C and D are not triggers recognised by IAS 23.

questions.question: Calabar Ports Ltd borrowed N120 million at 15% per annum specifically for a warehouse. Construction, expenditure and borrowing began at the start of the year, and substantially all activities were complete at the end of month 10. The loan remained outstanding for the whole year. How much interest is capitalised for the year?
questions.explanation: Capitalisation stops when the asset is substantially complete, so 10 months is capitalised: N120 million x 15% x 10/12 = N15 million, and the last 2 months' interest is expensed. Option D capitalises the full year, option C is the 2 months that must be expensed, and option B uses 9 months.

questions.question: Which of the following must an entity disclose under IAS 23?

options.a: The interest rate it expects to pay next year
options.b: The amount of borrowing costs capitalised during the period and the capitalisation rate used
options.c: The names of the banks that provided the loans
options.d: The market value of the qualifying asset at the reporting date

questions.explanation: IAS 23 requires disclosure of the amount of borrowing costs capitalised during the period and the capitalisation rate used to determine the amount eligible for capitalisation. Options C, A and D are not disclosures required by IAS 23.

questions.question: Platinum Nigeria Limited has general borrowings outstanding all year: 10% loan of N10m, 5% debenture of N20m and 20% loan of N50m, giving a capitalisation rate of 15%. On its qualifying asset it spent N10m on 1 April and N40m on 1 June, the start of construction being 1 April. For the year ended 31 December, how much borrowing cost is recognised as an expense?
questions.explanation: Total interest is N1m + N1m + N10m = N12m. The capitalised part is N10m x 15% x 9/12 = N1,125,000 plus N40m x 15% x 7/12 = N3,500,000, which is N4,625,000, so N12,000,000 - N4,625,000 = N7,375,000 is expensed. N4,500,000 wrongly treats both amounts as outstanding for the full 12 months, but interest before construction began on 1 April cannot be capitalised.

questions.question: A company in Lagos borrows in US dollars to build a factory. Under IAS 23, exchange differences arising on this foreign currency borrowing form part of borrowing costs

options.a: To the extent they are regarded as an adjustment to interest costs
options.b: In full, whether they are gains or losses on the loan
options.c: Never, because they are always taken directly to equity
options.d: Only when the loan is repaid before the factory is complete

questions.explanation: Borrowing costs include exchange differences on foreign currency borrowings only to the extent that they adjust the interest cost of the loan. Including them in full goes too far, because any part of the exchange difference beyond that adjustment is not a borrowing cost. Saying they are never included is also wrong, since IAS 23 lists them as one component of borrowing costs.

questions.question: An investment firm in Victoria Island uses borrowed money to buy shares quoted on the stock exchange. Why are these shares not a qualifying asset under IAS 23?

options.a: Financial assets are not qualifying assets
options.b: They were bought with general, not specific, borrowings
options.c: Only assets built for sale can be qualifying assets
options.d: The interest rate on the borrowing is too low

questions.explanation: IAS 23 states that financial assets, such as quoted shares, are not qualifying assets, so interest on money borrowed to buy them is expensed. Whether the funds came from general or specific borrowings affects how the capitalised amount is measured, not whether the asset qualifies. Limiting qualifying assets to items built for sale is wrong, because plants, power stations and investment properties built for use can also qualify.

questions.question: A shipbuilder in Apapa builds an ocean-going vessel for sale to a customer, a job that takes about 18 months. The vessel is held as inventory during construction. Can it be a qualifying asset under IAS 23?

options.a: No, because inventories can never be qualifying assets
options.b: Yes, but only if the funds came from a specific loan
options.c: Yes, inventories that take a substantial period to produce can qualify
options.d: No, because only assets for the entity's own use qualify

questions.explanation: A qualifying asset is one that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale, and inventories that take a long time to produce meet this test. Only inventories produced over a short period are excluded. The idea that inventories can never qualify confuses this long-production case with routine, quickly produced stock, and the type of borrowing does not decide whether an asset qualifies.
